000c7f50-ff95-5a24-b26f-2c2401107ffd.name: *Mosque of the Sultan, Cairo*
000c7f50-ff95-5a24-b26f-2c2401107ffd.short_description:
During the 1850s and 1860s, Francis Frith was one of England's most celebrated photographers. In September 1856, he set sail for Alexandria. This was the first of three trips that Frith would take to the Near East. The model was that of the 'Grand Tour'.  
Any analysis of Frith's work leads to the discourse of the tension between empirical knowledge and spiritual awareness in Victorian England. The photograph operated as a tool that could have moral influence upon those who viewed them with their ability to bring viewers to the locations of holy events.  
But even from a purely secular point of view, Frith's photographs become operators within an ideology specific to the era. Frith's thematic choices are manifest of the Victorians' tendency to regard themselves in relation to the larger history of mankind.
000c7f50-ff95-5a24-b26f-2c2401107ffd.dimensions: Height: 161 mm photograph, Width: 210 mm photograph
000c7f50-ff95-5a24-b26f-2c2401107ffd.author: Victoria and Albert Museum
keywords: Albumen process; Grand Tour; Holy Land; Victorian; Egypt; travel; history of photography

0066daed-f170-56db-b502-467e8b3e136c.name: Italian Company Breda Ernesto. Factory for Torpedoes and Navy Equipment, Milan. View of the Female Section of Lathes Division. Production of 75 mm Shrapnel Shells
0066daed-f170-56db-b502-467e8b3e136c.short_description:
Women working at lathes to make shrapnel shells in an Italian factory that produced torpedoes and other weapons. The war had an important impact on women’s work.  
As historian Perry Willson pointed out, during WWI “women rarely directly substituted for men, instead tending to move into new work roles produced by wartime expansion.”  
In Italy, the number of women who worked in factories producing weapons and ammunitions rose from 23,000 in 1915 to 198,000 in 1918. The numbers were far less than the women who participated in war production with more traditional “female roles”, such as making uniforms (400,000) or knitting woollen garments for the soldiers (200,000). However, Willson explained, women working in weapons’ factories had a relevance “as symbolic harbinger of change that greatly outweighed their actual numbers.”
0066daed-f170-56db-b502-467e8b3e136c.author: Cristina Mosillo, Giulia Barrera

007d6f6b-4f84-5cd4-97d4-b1637e409355.name: Emigrant family
007d6f6b-4f84-5cd4-97d4-b1637e409355.short_description: The 1923 population exchange between Greece and Turkey was based upon religious identity, and involved the Greek Orthodox citizens of Turkey and the Muslim citizens of Greece. The "Convention Concerning the Exchange of Greek and Turkish Populations" was signed at Lausanne, Switzerland, on 30 January 1923, by the governments of Greece and Turkey. This photo belongs to a Turkish family who migrated from Crete to Turkey in 1925.

00c8cda2-d033-5a89-89e5-4f6a4483e3da.name: The Hijaz Railway construction workers
00c8cda2-d033-5a89-89e5-4f6a4483e3da.short_description: The Hijaz Railway was a narrow-gauge railway (1,050mm/3ft, 5 11⁄32 in track gauge) that ran from Damascus to Medina, through the Hijaz region of Saudi Arabia, with a branch line to Haifa on the Mediterranean Sea. It was a part of the Ottoman railway network and was built to extend the line from the Haydarpaşa Terminal in Istanbul beyond Damascus to the holy city of Mecca. It got no further than Medina, 400 kilometres (250mi) short of Mecca, due to the interruption of the construction works caused by the outbreak of World War I.

01309821-1550-570d-b610-d7e90337db0f.name: Çırağan Palace
01309821-1550-570d-b610-d7e90337db0f.short_description: Pascal Sébah (1823-86) was a pioneer photographer who worked in Istanbul. In 1857 he opened his first photography studio in Istanbul. Çırağan Palace, built by Sultan Abdülâziz, was designed by the palace architect Nigoğayos Balyan and constructed by his sons Sarkis and Hagop Balyan between 1863 and 1867. This was a period in which all Ottoman sultans used to build their own palaces rather than using those of their ancestors. Çırağan Palace is the last example of this period. The inner walls and the roof were made of wood, the outer walls of colourful marble. The palace is connected with a beautiful marble bridge to the Yıldız Palace on the hill behind. A very high garden wall protects the palace from the outer world.
keywords: Photograph; Old İstanbul Photograph; İstanbul; Pascal Sebah

01a64f5c-ceca-5e43-b3af-115b31492d64.name: Portrait of Abraham Salamon De Camondo
01a64f5c-ceca-5e43-b3af-115b31492d64.short_description: The Camondo Family is a family of Spanish-Portuguese Jewish origin. Abraham Salomon Camondo, who was born in İstanbul in 1781, acted as the Ottoman government's banker before the establishment of the Ottoman Bank. He founded a bank called "*Isaac et Compagnie Camondo*" with his brother Isaac in 1815. The bank grew in a short time period into a reputable international financial institution. Camondo prospered greatly and became the prime banker to the Ottoman Empire until the founding of the Imperial Ottoman Bank in 1863. The bank had a close relationship with the business community and banks of London, Paris and the Vienna Stock Exchange. The bank had also funded defence needs of Ottoman Empire during the Crimean War.
01a64f5c-ceca-5e43-b3af-115b31492d64.holder: The Quincentennial Foundation Museum, Zulfaris Synagogue Museum

03110c09-4d62-5959-a659-ea8534ac6e28.name: Construction Site at Shellal
03110c09-4d62-5959-a659-ea8534ac6e28.short_description: In 1900, Count Giulio d’Aspremont, an Italian diplomat, visited the construction site of the first dam across the Nile (today known as the Aswan Low Dam or Old Aswan Dam). He took several pictures of the works and of the monuments on the island of Philae that were going to be submerged by the water. He published some of them on the *Bulletin of the Italian Geographical Society*, where he wrote that up to 2,000 Italian workers were employed in the works (as stone-cutters, miners and masons), out of a total labour force of about 10,000 or 12,000; an Italian village had sprung up on the Nile banks, with modest little houses, trattorias and shops.
03110c09-4d62-5959-a659-ea8534ac6e28.author: Patrizia Pampana

03762b34-622e-5cca-85b2-11ca849dd5d2.name: The Hijaz Railway delegations
03762b34-622e-5cca-85b2-11ca849dd5d2.short_description: The Hijaz Railway ran from Damascus to Medina, through the Hijaz region of Saudi Arabia, with a branch line to Haifa on the Mediterranean Sea. It was a part of the Ottoman railway network and was built to extend the line from the Haydarpaşa Terminal in Istanbul beyond Damascus to the holy city of Mecca. The main purpose of the railway was to establish a connection between the capital of the Ottoman Empire and the seat of the Islamic Caliphate, and Hijaz in Arabia, the site of the holiest shrines of Islam and the holy city of Mecca, the destination of the Hajj annual pilgrimage. Another important reason was to improve the economic and political integration of the distant Arabian provinces into the Ottoman state, and to facilitate the transportation of military forces.
03762b34-622e-5cca-85b2-11ca849dd5d2.holder: Istanbul University, Nadir Eserler Kütüphanesi (Rare Books Library)

0463649a-43f8-5ea7-b084-0c9df356d36f.description: The photograph postcard, Yıldırım Photocard no. 60, shows a freight or work train in a rocky mountain passage. The Yıldırım Army Group was formed in 1917 as a combined Ottoman-German command. It was originally conceived in connection with plans to recover Baghdad, but its operational focus shifted to the Palestine front.

057b0a91-5753-5a0f-a506-60b096d9eeb0.name: Saliha Sultan Fountain
057b0a91-5753-5a0f-a506-60b096d9eeb0.short_description: Robertson’s photographs of landscapes and monuments were usually printed in a roughly 25 by 30cm format. In the early years of his career as a photographer, he appears to have preferred the albumen-on-glass method of taking negatives, switching to the wet collodion process around 1855. For his positive prints, he used salt paper until about 1858; after that, prints were made on albumen paper even if they were made from negatives taken before that year. Robertson’s photographs are concentrated mainly in and around the districts known as Sultanahmet, Beyoğlu, Galata and Tophane today. This photo captures the Saliha Sultan Fountain in Galata.
057b0a91-5753-5a0f-a506-60b096d9eeb0.author: Bahattin Öztuncay
keywords: Photography; İstanbul; History of architecture

057cb072-73f1-5597-b0c3-f4145e5d0880.name: *British Soldiers Near Selimiye Barracks in Scutari Waiting to be Dispatched to Crimea*
057cb072-73f1-5597-b0c3-f4145e5d0880.short_description: Robertson's photographs of the Crimean War represent an important chapter in his career. The Crimean War was the first war in history to be extensively covered by press correspondents. The photographs taken by James Robertson and Roger Fenton put them in the ranks of the world’s first war photojournalists. James Robertson’s first photographs related to the Crimean War were actually taken in Istanbul. After England’s declaration of war on 27 March 1854, British and colonial forces dispatched to the front by sea began gathering at Selimiye in Üsküdar and neighbouring districts in April and May.
057cb072-73f1-5597-b0c3-f4145e5d0880.author: Bahattin Öztuncay
keywords: Crimean War; war photojounalism; British forces in Crimean War

069c2465-1b42-5572-8535-19f44b1fc837.name: Archaeological excavations
069c2465-1b42-5572-8535-19f44b1fc837.short_description:
This photograph shows the entrance to a tomb in the region of al-Kouban in Nubia, one of the archaeological sites excavated by James E. Quibell in 1882. The tomb has a vaulted ceiling made of mud brick, and the entrance marks the expansion of the tomb building from the inside.  
The photo is from a gelatine print negative, and it was included in the archive of the archaeological area of Saqqara, Giza.

06aabaa5-8fbd-543d-ac79-07b3315474de.name: The Statue of The God Bes
06aabaa5-8fbd-543d-ac79-07b3315474de.short_description: A large statue of dwarf God Bes is located in the Aessos Works Hall. Bes was an ancient Egyptian dwarf god. He was a complex being who was both a deity and a demonic fighter. He was a god of war, yet he was also a patron of childbirth and the home, and was associated with sexuality, humour, music and dancing. Bes also became popular with the Phoenicians and in Cyprus.

06eab576-316a-57c3-8710-45a77c94f15b.name: Alexandria: The Consuls’ Square Rebuilt
06eab576-316a-57c3-8710-45a77c94f15b.short_description: The large, rectangular square initially know under the French name “Place des Consuls” (later as Muhammad 'Ali Square), was officially inaugurated in 1860. It was designed by Francesco Mancini, chief engineer of the “Commissione d’ornato” (Board of Works), a committee set up in 1834 by Muhammad 'Ali (ruler of Egypt in 1805-1848), and modelled after similar urban-planning committees already functioning in some Italian cities. In 1872, an equestrian statue of Muhammad 'Ali was erected in the square, which took his name. In July 1882, after anti-foreign rioting in Alexandria, the British fleet heavily bombed the city, causing major destructions to the buildings surrounding the square.
06eab576-316a-57c3-8710-45a77c94f15b.author: Patrizia Pampana, Giulia Barrera

07024cd6-c5bb-5d57-96ec-903ad7f248c4.name: Museo Nazionale Preistorico Etnografico “L. Pigorini” (National Museum of Prehistory and Ethnography), Exhibition Room
07024cd6-c5bb-5d57-96ec-903ad7f248c4.short_description:
The origins, in terms of scientific activity and conservation, of the Museo Nazionale Preistorico Etnografico "Luigi Pigorini" in Rome, can be traced back to the foundation in 1875 of the “Regio Museo Nazionale Preistorico Etnografico di Roma" (Royal National Museum of Prehistory and Ethnography). Initially the museum was located in a wing of the Palazzo del Collegio Romano built in the late 16th century by the Society of Jesus.  
This rare image represents the old arrangement of one of the rooms of the Roman College, where the collection of antiquities and curiosities gathered together by Father Athanasius Kircher was kept after the foundation of the museum. According to the intentions of its founder, Luigi Pigorini, the purpose of this new institution was not only to gather together the remains of Italian prehistoric culture and the "primitive" cultures of other European and non-European peoples in a "central" museum located in the new capital of the Kingdom, but above all to support, promote and participate in research by paleontologists in Italy.

07024cd6-c5bb-5d57-96ec-903ad7f248c4.author: Mario Mineo, Marina Minozzi

0758a11b-67ab-5ddc-a953-275a1d7a45b8.description: This is a loose albumen print made from an original negative  by Bonfils. It shows a train at the Jaffa railway station with passengers ready to embark. Jaffa can be seen in the distance."Bonfils" and "1196 - Arrivée du train a Jaffa" on the print. From the Finn collection.  The track is the original metre-guage track and so the photograph is dated to before AH 1332 / AD 1914,  and as everything looks new, probably quite close to the date of construction in AH 1310 / AD 1892.   The train seems to consist of one of the Baldwin 2-6-0's locomotives, a couple of vans and two of the bogie carriages - a quite typical train combination.  The people in the picture may well have been station employees, posing for the photographer.

0a469d79-a94f-5097-a3cc-17e2bdc452a1.name: Balkan immigrants village at Sivrihisar
0a469d79-a94f-5097-a3cc-17e2bdc452a1.short_description: The civilian population living in the Balkans was forced to migrate to Anatolia due to the Balkan Wars at the end of the 18th century: the 1821 Mora rebellion, the 1856 Crimean war, the 1864 Russian-Caucasian war, the 1877-1878 Ottoman-Russian War, the 1896-97 Crete Rebellion, the 1912-13 Balkan Wars, World War I from 1914 to 1918 and the 1919-22 Greek-Turkish War. These wars resulted in mass migrations. The Ottoman Empire lost almost all its European territories west of the River Maritsa, drawing present day Turkey's western border. A large influx of Turks started to flee into the Ottoman heartland as a result of the lost lands. By 1914, the remaining core region of the Ottoman Empire had experienced a population increase of around 2.5 million because of the flood of immigration from the Balkans.

0b5e2b9b-6dd4-501c-9d61-0af91a0c8de8.short_description: The difficulties in returning to peacetime society after the end of the First World War created huge shifts in the social fabric of Paris. The city saw continuous strikes from May to July 1919. The most numerically significant was the steelworkers' strike, but all sectors were affected, as we can see from this photo, in which bank workers protest the "high cost of living" and "insufficient salaries".

0b654295-705f-5779-91d5-6ee361403ebb.name: Nouvelle gare de Haidar-Pacha. (New Haidar Pasha Station)
0b654295-705f-5779-91d5-6ee361403ebb.description: The postcard depicts the new Haidar-Pasha station, Constantinople. The first station before the new one was a modest structure appropriate to a relatively short suburban and regional railway. As the network expanded across Anatolia and the planning of the Baghdad Railway, the construction of the present station began in 1906. The architects were Otto Ritter and Hellmuth Cuno, and construction was undertaken by the German firm Philipp Holzmann. The station is a Neoclassical building that draws its symmetrical monumental composition, steep roofs, towers, stone façades and architectural vocabulary from European historicism. The postcard presents the station from the Bosporus, emphasising its monumental waterside façade. The building occupies an artificial platform at the edge of the sea and functions as an intermodal transport complex linking trains, ferries and port installations.

0b6eceea-2f90-5eb6-9483-03f0734b34dc.name: Misrata [Libya]. In the Home of Gabrielli, Agent of the Society of Maritime Services [Società dei servizi marittimi]
0b6eceea-2f90-5eb6-9483-03f0734b34dc.short_description:
In 19th and early 20th century Africa, the nature of the relations between European men and African women varied dramatically according to the different power relations between the partners. In colonial situations, the legal subordination of the colonised people put African women in particularly weak positions vis-à-vis European men, generally resulting in very exploitative relationships. In countries that were not under European rule, more balanced relationships could develop.  
This picture shows a mixed family in Libya before the onset of Italian colonialism. The setting of the picture suggests that the Libyan woman enjoyed respect and status within the family: the woman and her children are sitting on chairs, surrounded by persons who appear to be domestic servants, and the Italian man is standing behind her, looking at their children.

0c0afba6-5d14-5078-bcea-d6d65921461c.name: Passengers and onlookers waiting for the métropolitain at the Place de Bastille
0c0afba6-5d14-5078-bcea-d6d65921461c.short_description: Eugène Atget (1857–1927) began developing an interest in photography in 1888. He created his photos in series, and sold them to institutions. It was thus, that around 1898, he came to photograph the old neighbourhoods of Paris destined to demolition, and sold these photographs to the new Commission du Vieux Paris. As he photographed roads dug up by the urban excavations, he also captured onlookers fascinated by this new mode of transport. The Bastille station is pictured here, one of the overground sections of the ligne 1, which explains how these people were able to comfortably observe. The Colonne de Juillet of the Place de Bastille is visible in the background.
keywords: Cities; métropolitain; Paris

0c15121c-bdb4-5d29-91aa-079d86d55f11.name: Marseille: inauguration of M. Sanant's (Tunisia) exhibit - a picturesque corner of the West African pavilion
0c15121c-bdb4-5d29-91aa-079d86d55f11.short_description: In the latter half of the 19th century, many European countries held exhibitions about their colonies, both during world fairs and smaller events. France used world fairs to "showcase" their colonies, both in the great Paris world fairs as well as smaller, colonial fairs organised in Marseille (1906, 1922) and Paris (1931). These expositions glorified colonial expansion, particularly by offering visitors an "object lesson". Tunisia took the spotlight in 1906 due to the central role it played in the ongoing dispute with Italy. The "indigenous villages", such as the one pictured in this photograph, were above all representations of the way Europeans imagined their colonies. They were later described as "human zoos" by historians of the late 20th century, due to the horrific practice of putting people for display as if they were animals.
keywords: Expositions; colonise

0c667bca-0934-5597-9606-a0052b8b5720.name: *Cairo, the Nile Dam*
0c667bca-0934-5597-9606-a0052b8b5720.short_description: The reign of Muhammad 'Ali Pasha was marked by a series of great changes, including attempts to take control of irrigation. The governor appointed French specialists, amongst whom was Linant de Bellefonds, and tasked them with the construction of a dam near Cairo. Linant de Bellefonds faced a great many difficulties during the construction, such as saving the pyramids, which the Pasha had wanted to destroy in order to supply the new dam with stone. The works were taken over by the engineer Eugène Mougel who added fortifications, as can be seen from this photograph, taken by a tourist at the beginning of the 20th century. The dam was completed c. 1835.
keywords: Irrigation; dams; Egypt

0cd36a65-5e7b-5bb2-8525-edcaea12dea2.name: Omar al-Mukhtar (1861–1931), leader of anticolonial resistance in Libya
0cd36a65-5e7b-5bb2-8525-edcaea12dea2.short_description:
In 1923, the head of the Senussi Muslim order Mohamed Idris charged Omar al-Mukhtār (1861-1931) with the task of leading Libyan anti-colonial resistance. Omar al-Mukhtār was leader of the Libyan anti-Italian guerrillas, until he was captured and executed by the Italians in 1931.  
In 1911-12, Italy successfully waged war against Turkey for the colonial conquest of Libya. However, during WWI Italy lost control of most of the Libyan territory. After the war, it took Italy about ten years to re-establish its hold on Libyan inland areas.  
Thanks to his military genius, to the wide popular support he enjoyed and the financial help provided by the Senussia, Omar al-Mukhtār was able to keep the Italians in check for years, even when the army of the invaders was ten times larger than the guerrilla forces. The Italians were able to capture him only after deporting part of the population of the Cyrenaica mountains (Gebel Akhda) in concentration camps on the coast.
0cd36a65-5e7b-5bb2-8525-edcaea12dea2.author: Giulia Barrera

0cdaaac9-facc-525a-b1f1-756e4b6df842.name: Silvio Benigno Crespi and his family in the courtyard of Villa Pia (Villa Crespi), Orta San Giulio (Novara)
0cdaaac9-facc-525a-b1f1-756e4b6df842.short_description:
Silvio Benigno Crespi was one of the children of Cristoforo Benigno Crespi, the industrialist who built a Moorish-style villa (known as villa Pia or villa Crespi) built on the lake d’Orta.  
This picture was taken in the courtyard of Villa Crespi. It shows Silvio Benigno Crespi (standing, on the right); sitting on the extreme left is his wife Teresa Ghiglieri; at the centre their first-born child Benigno and their other six children.  
The picture gives a hint of the lifestyle of this stock of cultivated, enlightened and successful industrialists.
0cdaaac9-facc-525a-b1f1-756e4b6df842.author: Ignazio Galella

0df04b1e-0995-5f3a-a767-e848e62c8fbf.name: *The Bridge Carol I*
0df04b1e-0995-5f3a-a767-e848e62c8fbf.short_description: The railroad bridge over the Danube that was built between 1890–1895 in South-Eastern Romania shortened the route of the Orient Express, a passenger train meant to connect Paris to Istanbul. The bridge made it possible for the Orient Express to reach Constanţa, a Black Sea port, from where ships went to Istanbul, whereas in the past the journey implied people being ferried on the Danube from Romania to Bulgaria, travelling by train to Varna (a Bulgarian Black Sea port) and then taking a ship to Istanbul. The “Carol I” bridge, which was designed by engineer Anghel Saligny and was at that time the longest in Europe, was inaugurated on 29 September 1895. In his inaugural speech, the king declared that “Romania is now owner of the shortest route between the northern seas and the countries of the Orient”.

0e8bab0f-566b-5c60-b111-2262460c62b8.name: Control Tower Airport Basrah
0e8bab0f-566b-5c60-b111-2262460c62b8.description: Postcard; printed; monochrome real photograph showing the airport control tower, Basra, flying the national flag
0e8bab0f-566b-5c60-b111-2262460c62b8.obtention: Bought on ebay; presented by St John Simpson

0ec0000a-9f1f-5af3-8461-b9f66f7fbd90.name: Souvenir des Relations télegraphiques entre Damas, Hedjaz, Damas (Syrie). (Memorial Column of Telegraphic Connections between Damascus and Hijaz, Damascus, Syria)
0ec0000a-9f1f-5af3-8461-b9f66f7fbd90.description: The Amud al Telegraph (the Telegraph Column or Telegraph Monument), sometimes locally known as Amud al Marjeh, is situated at the centre of Marjeh Square in Damascus. The monument was designed in 1900 by Raimondo D’Aronco and erected in Marjeh Square in 1904. It was constructed to commemorate the completion of the telegraph line linking Istanbul, Damascus and Mecca. The monument's bronze shaft is decorated with stylized representations of telegraph wires, poles and related equipment. The small structure at the top of the column is a model of the Yıldız Hamidiye Mosque in Istanbul, located near Yıldız Palace. The column formed the centrepiece of the redesign of Marjeh Square, transforming an open riverside space along the Barada River into a civic focal point, a transportation hub and a symbolic administrative centre.
0ec0000a-9f1f-5af3-8461-b9f66f7fbd90.bibliography:
Weber, Stefan, *Damascus: Ottoman Modernity and Urban Transformation (1808–1918)*, 2 vols, Aarhus: Aarhus University Press, 2009.  
  
Aga Khan Trust for Culture, *Historic Train Stations of the Al-Hijaz Railway Network*, Geneva: Aga Khan Trust for Culture, 2004.  
  
Shihabi, Qutayba, *Muʿjam Dimashq al-Tārīkhī*, Damascus: Ministry of Culture, 1999.
keywords: Syria; Monument; Photograph; transportation

0f088fa7-47b1-5825-9ada-f45bc3097162.name: The Italian Politeama Rossini theatre in Tunis, inaugurated in 1903
0f088fa7-47b1-5825-9ada-f45bc3097162.short_description:
The Politeama Rossini was built by the construction company of Giuseppe Di Vittorio (a Sicilian who had migrated to Tunisia in 1882); the architect was a Mr. Baron. It could house an audience of 2,500.  
The first Italian theatre in Tunis was the “Teatro Tapia” founded in 1826. Other Italian theatres (such as the “Teatro Italiano” and the “Teatro Paradiso”) and concert halls (“Gran Teatro”, “Teatro Cohen”, etc.) were created in Tunis the following decades.
0f088fa7-47b1-5825-9ada-f45bc3097162.author: Giulia Barrera

0f8edbbb-ebb5-5b6a-b92d-27d539424298.name: Drawing water from a well in the village of Tell Halula (Syria)
0f8edbbb-ebb5-5b6a-b92d-27d539424298.description: This image serves to illustrate the day-to-day existence of communities inhabiting arid regions of Syria. It portrays a local woman engaged in the collection of water from a well, thus offering a glimpse into the domestic practices of these communities. As demonstrated in the background, the architectural design of the local construction is informed by the availability of materials in the immediate area. The architectural style employed is a simple and functional house type that has been adapted to provide protection for the local communities against the high temperatures typically experienced in the region.
0f8edbbb-ebb5-5b6a-b92d-27d539424298.author: Yelyzaveta Basysta
keywords: Water; Tell Halula; Syria; well.

0fae2309-f11c-5cf4-a9a0-0bd126c69093.name: A picture from the very beginning
0fae2309-f11c-5cf4-a9a0-0bd126c69093.description: The oldest photograph in the collection of the National Museum is in essence a photo montage. Johann Baptist Isenring assembled this group picture from different photographs of unidentified men – this is particularly discernible in the different sized heads. The photographer touched up the boundaries of the individual component photographs and coloured the composite. Johann Baptist Isenring was one of the first Swiss photographers. He mounted the first photographic exhibition in St. Gall as early as 1840.
keywords: Photo montage; Photogenic Drawing; Johan Baptist Isenring; St Gall
materials: Photo montage, Salt-paper print, coloured, Photogenetic Drawing

10750e4a-16c1-59c9-9ca2-1fd0ff0f88a6.name: Palace of the Emir Bashir Shihab II
10750e4a-16c1-59c9-9ca2-1fd0ff0f88a6.description: The image depicts the principal courtyard of Beiteddine Palace, featuring a circular stone fountain. The construction of the Beiteddine Palace was initiated in 1788 under the authority of Emir Bashir Shihab II, who ruled Mount Lebanon during the Ottoman period, and was largely completed by 1812. The palace functioned as an administrative and residential complex and is an important example of Ottoman-influenced architecture in the Levant. The surrounding façades are constructed from coursed limestone masonry and incorporate arcaded galleries, staircases and balconies with wooden railings and decorated door and window surrounds. Today, the Beiteddine Palace is a major cultural heritage site and tourist destination. It houses museum collections and hosts cultural events, contributing to its continued use as a site of historical interpretation and public engagement.
10750e4a-16c1-59c9-9ca2-1fd0ff0f88a6.author: Yelyzaveta Basysta
keywords: Water; Palace; Beiteddine; Ottoman.

11e4d236-bdc2-5339-827e-8d983887fbd6.short_description: Private carriage of Queen Maria Pia, offered by her father, King Victor Emmanuel, when she married the Portuguese king D. Louis in 1862. The chariot is pulled by steam locomotive D. Luiz.

139d89ef-83f7-5902-8e15-21a9ae45cbf2.name: Early collecting
139d89ef-83f7-5902-8e15-21a9ae45cbf2.short_description: A colossal statue of Cypriot Bes was found near the agora of the ancient city of Amathus in 1863. The British government attempted to obtain it for the British Museum but it was sent to Constantinople on order of the Porte. This illustrates the beginnings of a more official policy to claim antiquities for the Ottoman state and to exhibit them in museums. The first Ottoman Law on antiquities was passed in 1869, followed by a more detailed one in 1874.
keywords: museums

13b9879f-22ab-5095-b41e-67ba673be224.name: Set of photos illustrating the Insects Hall, the Worms Hall and the Snake Hall at Fu`ad Agricultural Museum
13b9879f-22ab-5095-b41e-67ba673be224.short_description: The Fu`ad Agriculture Museum was considered the first of its kind in the Middle East and the Arab World during the 1930s. It was inaugurated during the time of King Faruq, the son of King Fu`ad, and houses a large number of collections related to agricultural and rural environments, as well as agricultural plants and animals.

13c7b9a9-f604-53fe-8a42-508a3f774e73.short_description: General view of the pyramids of Abusir with a group of workers excavating the pyramids of Sahure and Niuserre as part of the German archaeological mission in 1901.

147b289f-3d6e-58be-8aa0-db105cfb150f.name: *National Museum of Archaeology No. 9 (Arab Courtyard) Monuments and Epigraphy of Islamic Spain*
147b289f-3d6e-58be-8aa0-db105cfb150f.description: View of the courtyard in the National Museum of Archaeology, also known as "Arab courtyard", between 1917-1936. This room displayed different pieces such as the Alfajería arch, a copy of the fountain of the Lions and the bronze lamp from the Alhambra palace. This room was one of the first museum galleries focusing on Arab or Islamic pieces in Europe.

158e0a7a-2ff1-5a91-9653-24fcf9372ba0.name: Photographic view of Mecca
158e0a7a-2ff1-5a91-9653-24fcf9372ba0.short_description: Safouh Izzat Naamani was born in Beirut in 1926 and very early on became fascinated by photography. He first travelled to Saudi Arabia in 1951 in order to photograph political events and in 1954 travelled to Mecca specifically to photograph the Masjid al-Haram and the Hajj. Naamani was one of the first photographers to capture Hajj from the air and his aerial photographs of Hajj and Mecca are unique in this period. His photographs from the 1960s capture the newly expanding sanctuary. This photograph was taken during the second phase of the Saudi extension, during the reign of King Faisal (r. 1964–1975). The photograph clearly shows the newly covered Safa-Marwa area for *sa‘i* in construction; also visible is the imposing Jabal al-Nur to the right of the skyline.
158e0a7a-2ff1-5a91-9653-24fcf9372ba0.holder: Khalili Family Trust – Hajj and the Arts of Pilgrimage Collection
158e0a7a-2ff1-5a91-9653-24fcf9372ba0.method_for_datation: Information regarding date supplied by the photographer's family.
158e0a7a-2ff1-5a91-9653-24fcf9372ba0.author: Qaisra Khan
keywords: Hajj; Hijaz; Holy place; Ka'ba; Medina; Mosque; paper; Pilgrimage; Prayer; Prophet Muhammad; Religion; Mecca; photograph

159f7828-e467-5f3d-b3ba-96aafc6f5b7c.name: Postcard: *Colonial Exhibition 1907, Tuareg caravan*
159f7828-e467-5f3d-b3ba-96aafc6f5b7c.description:
This postcard (not franked or used) is part of a collection donated by the anthropologist Manuel Antón.  
During the second half of the nineteenth century in Europe and America there were held countless ethnological and colonial exhibitions that showed groups of individuals from distant exotic territories, to make them public and available to anthropologists and scholars. They were put on show alongside exotic animals and recreations of the structures inhabited by these people in their places of origin.  
These exhibitions were a result of the intensification of colonial imperialism of the West and also the relative popularity of two young scientific disciplines (physical anthropology and ethnology) and the development of new and intense forms of consumerism among the European bourgeoisie. Actually these exhibitions got to transmit a sense of lower and "savage" status of the colonised people (Sánchez Gómez, L. “Espectáculos demasiado humanos”, 2008, 88-89).
keywords: Exhibition; Photography

161d25a6-f2f3-5bd7-9bce-84afb082e31e.name: The Hijaz Railway Delegations
161d25a6-f2f3-5bd7-9bce-84afb082e31e.short_description: The Hijaz Railway ran from Damascus to Medina, through the Hijaz region of Saudi Arabia, with a branch line to Haifa on the Mediterranean Sea. It was a part of the Ottoman railway network and was built to extend the line from the Haydarpaşa Terminal in Istanbul beyond Damascus to the holy city of Mecca. The main purpose of the railway was to establish a connection between the capital of the Ottoman Empire and the seat of the Islamic Caliphate, and Hijaz in Arabia, the site of the holiest shrines of Islam and the holy city of Mecca, the destination of the Hajj annual pilgrimage. Another important reason was to improve the economic and political integration of the distant Arabian provinces into the Ottoman state, and to facilitate the transportation of military forces.
161d25a6-f2f3-5bd7-9bce-84afb082e31e.holder: Istanbul University, Nadir Eserler Kütüphanesi (Rare Books Library)
161d25a6-f2f3-5bd7-9bce-84afb082e31e.dates: Late 19th century – beginning of the 20th century
keywords: Yıldız Album; II. Abdulhamid Han; Photograph The Hijaz Railways

171d0c66-d91f-50c5-9daf-466b883aab37.name: Oussman Gassi, King of Bundu, 42 years, born in Sendou
171d0c66-d91f-50c5-9daf-466b883aab37.short_description: The villages inhabited by African and Asian immigrants attracted a great deal of attention during the time of the European world fairs. Even the sciences (medicine, anthropology, etc.) showed much curiosity towards them, a curiosity whose justification as 'scientific' seems incongruous and dishonest to a modern audience.
keywords: World fairs; Paris

179af9eb-b888-57e9-b30c-78f45dee8021.name: *Weapons Market Street*
179af9eb-b888-57e9-b30c-78f45dee8021.short_description: A rare photo of the weapons market street that goes back more than 700 years and is located in the Darb al-Ahmar area, to the North of Cairo. It was originally called “Al-`Izzi Market”, after a relative to Prince `Izz al-Din Bahdar, one of the Bahri Mamluks who was said to live there. With the passing of time, people started calling it “Suq al-Silah" street because of its many workshops and factories that made a variety of different weapons, including spears, swords and shields. The street provided weapons to the Citadel during the Mamluk era in Egypt.
keywords: Weapons Market; Cairo Markets; Old Cairo

17b041f8-8464-54a0-bfab-c18e51639102.name: A rare photo showing important guests at the inauguration of Luxor–Aswan Railway Line
17b041f8-8464-54a0-bfab-c18e51639102.short_description: A group of guests at the inauguration of the Luxor–Aswan Railway Line upon disembarking at the Station of Aswan. One of the rare photos for the inauguration of the Luxor–Aswan railway line, with `Adli Yakan Pasha; Muhammad Najib al-Gharabli Pasha; Husayn Rushdi Pasha; Tharwat Pasha; Fathallah Barakat Pasha; Morkos Hanna Pasha; al-Dagwi Bek, director of Aswan; and Mahmud Shakir Bek, deputy undersecretary of the Ministry of Transportation in attendance, in 1926.

17ebadf5-f8b4-5fec-89b1-0d6719047eeb.name: Uadi-Merdùm [Wadi Merdum]. Count Sforza and the Interpreter Maffei Transcribe a Roman Inscription Brought to their Attention by 'Natives'
17ebadf5-f8b4-5fec-89b1-0d6719047eeb.short_description:
In 1911, before the war broke out, Count Sforza and Ignazio Sanfilippo were touring Libya on a mission to assess local resources, sponsored by the Libyan branch of the Banco di Roma. Their parallel interest in Roman archaeology – testified by this photo – is meaningful for the connection between Italians’ claims of their Roman heritage and Italian colonial ambitions.  
In the opinion of Italian colonialists the discovery of Roman antiquities in Libya brought support to Italian argument that Italy had an historic right to rule over Libya.
17ebadf5-f8b4-5fec-89b1-0d6719047eeb.author: Patrizia Pampana, Giulia Barrera

184eef10-6e1e-5cd3-9d3c-79a146221593.name: Amelia del Valle y Serrano
184eef10-6e1e-5cd3-9d3c-79a146221593.description: The Marquis of Cerralbo (politician, historian, and collector of art and antiques) and his family visited Istanbul in 1889, and nowadays the Cerralbo Museum holds an interesting variety of pieces bought and collected as souvenirs from the family trip. When visiting a foreign country or city, being portraited by a famous photographer of studio was indispensable. In this case the photographers are the world-renowned Armenian Abdullah Frères, Photographes de S. M. I. le Sultan. This albumen portrait of Amelia del Valle y Serrano is delicate and quiet, with outstanding deep chocolate colour which reveals the quality of the photographic technique and the good condition of the object.
184eef10-6e1e-5cd3-9d3c-79a146221593.author: Cecilia Casas Desantes
keywords: Portrait; women; souvenir; memorabilia

185ba5fa-c953-5b73-a895-436fd368117e.name: Ottoman Clothing Album
185ba5fa-c953-5b73-a895-436fd368117e.short_description: With the political developments of the 19th century, interest in the East increased steadily in the western world. Everything belonging to the East was the centre of interest for western observers. As a result, close to 160 artists visited Istanbul in the 19th century. Pascal Sébah (1823-86) was a pioneer photographer who worked in Istanbul. Sébah opened a photography studio known as "El Chark " in Pera in 1857. The studio's most successful period started with the Vienna Universal Exhibition in 1873. Sébah formed a partnership with Joaillier Polycarpe in 1885. In 1899, the two partners bought Abdullah Frères's archives. For the Vienna Universal Exhibition in 1873, Pascal Sébah prepared *The Ottoman Clothing Album* to be exhibited at the Ottoman Stand.
185ba5fa-c953-5b73-a895-436fd368117e.holder: Istanbul University, Nadir Eserler Kütüphanesi (Rare Books Library)
185ba5fa-c953-5b73-a895-436fd368117e.dates: Late 19th century – beginning of the 20th century
keywords: Yıldız Album; II. Abdulhamid Han; Photograph Ancient Istanbul; Pascal Sebah

1959666e-3460-5e95-bc55-a3706388cf52.name: Archaeological excavations
1959666e-3460-5e95-bc55-a3706388cf52.short_description: This photograph documents the discovery and excavation of archaeological relics in the area of Saqqara in 1901. The original photograph was included in a specific collection of the German Archive.

19adb7d5-92bf-5c8a-8b63-f8d677d0e713.name: Danilo I, Prince of Montenegro (1871–1939)
19adb7d5-92bf-5c8a-8b63-f8d677d0e713.short_description: Danilo I, Prince of Montenegro (1871–1939) was the eldest son of King Nicola I of Montenegro. He was married to Princess Jutta von Mecklenburg-Strelitz and had to leave Montenegro after it was integrated in the kingdom of Yugoslavia after WWI. He died in 1937 in Vienna, Austria – in exile.
keywords: Danilo I, Prince of Montenegro; Jugoslavia; Vienna; Austria

1a9d55b4-313f-59d7-be4b-49e6c35ea73f.name: A train in the Taurus mountain crossing a bridge
1a9d55b4-313f-59d7-be4b-49e6c35ea73f.description: In the Taurus Mountains of southern Anatolia, a steam locomotive hauls freight wagons across a bridge, on one of the most difficult sections of the Baghdad Railway. To carry the railway from Anatolia southward towards Syria and eventually Mesopotamia, engineers had to negotiate the harsh terrain of steep hills and narrow valleys of the Taurus range. The construction required a succession of bridges, rock cuttings and tunnels where the track is carried along a deep rocky gap on a bridge curving along the mountainside.
1a9d55b4-313f-59d7-be4b-49e6c35ea73f.bibliography:
Great Britain Foreign Office, "Baghdad Railway: Route and Construction through the Taurus Mountains," Constantinople, August 23, 1912. India Office Records, British Library, Qatar Digital Library.  
  
McMurray, Jonathan S, *Distant Ties: Germany, the Ottoman Empire, and the Construction of the Baghdad Railway*, Westport, CT: Praeger, 2001.
keywords: Baghdad Railway; Taurus Mountains; railway bridge; steam locomotive; mountain railway

1ae05213-6e13-5660-a8b1-a4fa3e9ae5fe.name: Laying of the last rail in Damascus on June 25, 1895
1ae05213-6e13-5660-a8b1-a4fa3e9ae5fe.description: Photograph showing the laying of the last rail of the Beirut-Damascus railway, a 147km feat of railway engineering inaugurated in August 1895. Financed primarily by French and Belgian investors and sanctioned by the Ottoman Empire, it was the first major railway in the Levant, predating the Hijaz Railway by 13 years. The railway served as a vital economic link for 80 years, transforming towns like Aley and Bhamdoun into popular summer resorts, until its closure in 1976 following the outbreak of the Lebanese Civil War. Today, the route remains a landmark of industrial heritage. The photograph is by Maison Bonfils, one of the most prolific photographic studios of the 19th century Arab world, based in Beirut and active between 1867 and 1918.
1ae05213-6e13-5660-a8b1-a4fa3e9ae5fe.dimensions: Sheet: Height: 34 cm, width: 44 cm; Image: Height: 20 cm, 27,5 cm
1ae05213-6e13-5660-a8b1-a4fa3e9ae5fe.author: Giulia Martini
keywords: Albumen prints; Railways; Middle East; 20th Century

1af2dd04-8576-5d3d-9ef0-7c42ddce54b3.name: Bijâr Naṣîf [graphic] : Befestigte Station der Ḥiggâzbahn, 74 km nördlich von Medina, 489 m ü. M. 1910.
1af2dd04-8576-5d3d-9ef0-7c42ddce54b3.alternate_name: Abyār Naṣīf : Fastening station of the Hijaz railroad, 74 km north of Medina, 489 m above sea level. 1910. eng
1af2dd04-8576-5d3d-9ef0-7c42ddce54b3.description: This photograph translates to “Abyār Naṣīf : Fastening station of the Hijaz railroad, 74 km north of Medina, 489 m above sea level. 1910“ taken by Moritz Bernhard, and represents plate 62 in the portfolio: Bilder aus Palästina. Nord-Arabien und dem Sinai published in Berlin : Dietrich Riemer in 1916. It shows the tents of Ottoman soldiers at a site 74 kilometers from Medina across the Hijaz Railway. The literal translation of “Befestigte Station “ is “fortified station“, suggesting a defensive camp to protect the Hijaz Railway. Bijar Nasif also had a water reservoir, which adds to the importance of the station along the Hijaz Railway. The date of the publication of the image in 1916 also coincides with a passage by T. E. Lawrence in the book “Lawrence of Arabia’s Secret Dispatches “ where, in a report dated 30 October 1916, T. E. Lawrence identified Bir Nasif and Buwat as targets of a major assault planned by Faisal against the Hijaz Railway, to be coordinated with Arab advances towards Medina.

1c7eb8dd-c27a-55e4-b4bd-256860c07387.name: Types of Cairo
1c7eb8dd-c27a-55e4-b4bd-256860c07387.short_description: The historical photos, belonging to Enrico H. Giglioli's collection, were collected by the Florentine naturalist during his travel around the world in 1865–68 on the Magenta's steam corvette, with the purpose to start diplomatic and commercial relations. The "genre" images seem to be created "ad hoc" to represent human diversity along the different ages. The ethnographic photographs in the Giglioli's collection are part of the historical archive of the Pigorini Museum, and are very important for the history of anthropological science and history of photography. The origins in terms of scientific activity and conservation of Museo Nazionale Preistorico Etnografico "Luigi Pigorini" in Rome, can be traced back to the foundation in 1875 of the "Royal National Museum of Prehistory and Ethnography in Rome" within the buildings of the Roman College.

1deb708b-ab5d-5f99-8702-421204b044cf.name: Berber woman (Nailiya) lying down
1deb708b-ab5d-5f99-8702-421204b044cf.description: The image depicts a Nailiya, a woman of the Berber tribe of the Ouled Naïl, in the south of Algeria. She is lying on her side like an odalisque, wearing a colourful silk dress and the rich jewels used to perform their traditional dance. The Nailiyat were independent women, free to marry men of their choosing. They moved to the cities in the North to earn money as dancers, in order to maintain their families in their community of origin. All this was not fully understood by Europeans. With the emergence of sex-tourism these women were forced to introduce sexual content in their originally hieratic performance, and finally they were even considered as prostitutes by the French administration, which in turn led to them being repudiated in their villages. Early photography contributed to forge this image of the Nailiyat in the European imagination.
keywords: Photography; Orientalism; Algeria; Women

1e650671-cb20-50f3-8f15-8ed06e41849a.name: The Old Woman from Candia [Heraklion, Crete, Greece], the Only Person who Remained in Apollonia on the Day of the Occupation
1e650671-cb20-50f3-8f15-8ed06e41849a.short_description:
This picture was taken by an Italian military unit during the Italian invasion of Libya.  
Apollonia was the name of an ancient town, dating back to the 7th century BC. By 1911, Apollonia was nothing more than an archaeological site. The modern Arab town was called Marsa Susa. The Italians’ use of the ancient name was intended to remind readers that Libya was once under Roman rule. Italian colonialists claimed that Italy had an historic right to rule over Libya, since the Roman Empire once ruled over that country.

1e8d0442-f4d0-543b-99bd-eef31229b6e9.description: The views of towns and tourist attractions by British photographer Francis Frith were extremely sought-after in the second half of the 19th century. He sold large numbers of his photographs, such as this view of the town of Lausanne, and ran a company working internationally. On the one hand, his success was based on the need of the developing tourism sector for images and souvenirs. On the other hand, Frith saw things in ways familiar from graphic images and painting.

202cc823-091f-52bb-b0fd-9a166d692b86.name: Constantinople. Inauguration de la ligne d´Eregli en 1905 et Turkhan Pacha (Inauguration of the Eregli Line in 1905 with Turhan Pasha)
202cc823-091f-52bb-b0fd-9a166d692b86.description: The postcard depicts the inauguration of the Konya–Ereğli railway section, with Turhan Pasha among the Ottoman officials assembled for the ceremony. Although the postcard is dated 1905, archival records establish that the official opening took place at Ereğli Station on 25 October 1904. The Konya–Ereğli section constituted the first completed part of the Baghdad Railway project, and its inauguration was deliberately scheduled for the birthday of Sultan Abdülhamid II. Turhan Pasha, who was then Minister of Imperial Foundations (Evkaf-ı Hümayun Nazırı), headed the official delegation sent from Istanbul.

20b75da3-3556-540c-a1f6-b0db4ca7d41f.name: A view of London
20b75da3-3556-540c-a1f6-b0db4ca7d41f.short_description:
A stereograph is a pair of photographic images of the same subject taken from slightly different angles. This gives the illusion of a single three-dimensional image when viewed through a stereoscope designed to hold it. Stereographs were mass produced. Viewing them was a popular amusement carried out in the home from the 1850s until the early 20th century.  
This stereograph is from a series entitled 'Instantaneous Views of London'. The word 'instantaneous' reveals that an important selling-point for such photographs was that they quickly captured a moment in time. In this case the crowd and carriages of a busy London street are frozen in motion.
20b75da3-3556-540c-a1f6-b0db4ca7d41f.author: Victoria and Albert Museum
keywords: London; Buildings; Cathedrals; Streets; St Paul's Cathedral; Cityscapes; stereoscopic photography; stereoscope; stereograph

Pascal Sébah (1823-86) was a pioneer photographer who worked in Istanbul. Sébah opened a photography studio known as "El Chark " in Pera in 1857. 2372c4f0-19e9-5eec-8cf1-a0abc23e9648.name: Photographic views of Hajj, by Muhammad Sadiq Bey
2372c4f0-19e9-5eec-8cf1-a0abc23e9648.short_description:
Muhammad Sadiq Bey who was the first person to take photographs of Mecca, Medina and the Hajj. An Egyptian army engineer and surveyor, he was also the treasurer of the Egyptian Hajj caravan, travelling numerous times to the Hijaz. Using a technique first invented in the 1850s, Sadiq Bey took his first photographs in 1861 using glass plate negatives, especially useful for large-format frames. His photographs are often signed and dated in the negative. His most important photographs, of both the buildings and interior of the sanctuaries at Mecca and Medina, as well as sites at Arafat and Mina, were taken in 1880 and 1881. For the first time, the pilgrimage and the holy cities were precisely and realistically documented. Sadiq Bey’s photographic achievements were recognized by both the Arab and European world and in 1881 he won a gold medal at the Venice Geographical Exhibition. He published two important works: The *Mash‘al al-Mahmal* (The Torch of the Mahmal) in 1881, and *Dalil al-Hajj* (The Guide to the Hajj) in 1896, both of which included his photographs and observations of his journeys. Twelve of his photographs are in the Collection.  
\[arc.pp 211.9\] A view of Medina showing the Bab al-Shami on the North side of the city. Built within the city’s stone wall, the large gateway was one of three that allowed access into the town. In the centre of the photograph is the green dome built above the tomb of the Prophet Muhammad.  
\[arc.pp 211.4\] A view of the Ka‘ba surrounded by pilgrims performing the tawaf. The *mizab* (rainwater spout) is clearly discernable at the top of the Ka‘ba, whilst the Mosque of Bilal can be seen high upon the hilltop behind. The photograph is signed in and dated in Arabic, in the lower right hand corner.

2372c4f0-19e9-5eec-8cf1-a0abc23e9648.author: Qaisra Khan

23fa41ec-b0ae-57aa-b230-d5ba2e0f4a72.name: Air route to Baghdad via Amman and the desert. Rutba wells. The half way desert station. Seen from high altitude
23fa41ec-b0ae-57aa-b230-d5ba2e0f4a72.description: Photographed from an aircraft window around 1932 by the Photo Department of the American Colony in Jerusalem, this image shows Rutba Wells, the halfway station on the desert route between Amman and Baghdad. A square walled fort sits alone on the flat plain, with a few vehicles beside it and a single aeroplane waiting on the airstrip. Built for Imperial Airways, the fort served as a rest house on the air route from Britain to India, and it was guarded by Iraqi soldiers. The same walls also sheltered travellers crossing the desert overland, as well as camel caravans.

24203624-e517-513d-988d-06f0d9b1828a.short_description: The roots of 'labour day' go back to the 19th century, when strikers campaigned for an 8-hour working day. The events quickly escalated, and came to a head in Fourmies, France, in 1891. From then on, labour day protesters began wearing a red flower on the first of May in memory of their fallen comrades. This flower was later replaced by a sprig of lily of the valley in Île-de-France, which also commemorates the start of spring.

25019945-0006-566a-b1cc-e378a23e92ea.name: Farrokh Khan, Persian ambassador
25019945-0006-566a-b1cc-e378a23e92ea.short_description: Diplomatic relations between France and Persia were strained at the beginning of the 19th century, so Persia began to turn more and more to Great Britain. However, following a disagreement with Great Britain over the city of Herat, Persia re-established its diplomatic relationship with France. The ambassador Farrokh Khan was sent to Paris in the midst of the Anglo-Persian war (1856–57), and Napoléon III's diplomatic aid led to the Treaty of Paris (1857) and successfully ended the conflict. Félix Nadar, one of the most famous portrait photographers in Paris, photographed Farrokh Khan for the occasion.
keywords: Diplomacy; France; Persia

25615117-b95e-51bc-bba3-33731c28624f.name: Portrait of a young woman
25615117-b95e-51bc-bba3-33731c28624f.description: A young woman on the photograph poses in the interior, lying on the Pirot kilim. She is wearing an overcoat named *džube*, which belongs to traditional urban dress ensemble worn in Kosovo. For this occasion *džube* is turned into an evening dress and combined with modern accessories. The outfit was most probably worn at a costume ball, which was a popular practice at this time, related to the elements of traditional 19th century urban dress. The kilim on the photo is decorated with the *Crown Prince* (*prestolonaslednik*) ornament.
25615117-b95e-51bc-bba3-33731c28624f.author: Draginja Maskareli

257442d0-cc8b-5f59-9bdf-31aeac1cd79c.name: Postcard of Khan Antoun Bey Square
257442d0-cc8b-5f59-9bdf-31aeac1cd79c.short_description: Located next to the port, the Khan Antoun Bey Square was the entrance to the city for those arriving by sea. By the 19th century the *khan* itself, pictured here, housed trading offices on the ground and first floors and foreign consulates on the upper floors. The inner courtyard was used to park the consuls' horse-drawn carriages.

272951dc-4e51-55bc-bf53-6fb35a332aa6.name: Joint-stock company for iron, steel and railroad materials “Ferrotaie”. Factory for steel and railroad materials of Vado Ligure [Genoa, Italy]. Women working at milling machines
272951dc-4e51-55bc-bf53-6fb35a332aa6.short_description:
Women working in a steel and iron factory that produced materials of strategic value. The war had an important impact on women’s work. As historian Perry Willson pointed out, during WWI “women rarely directly substituted for men, instead tending to move into new work roles produced by wartime expansion.”  
In Italy, the number of women who worked in factories producing weapons and ammunitions rose from 23,000 in 1915 to 198,000 in 1918. Those numbers were far less than the women who participated in war production with more traditional “female roles”, such as making uniforms (400,000) or knitting woollen garments for the soldiers (200,000). However, Willson explained, women working in weapons’ factories had a relevance “as symbolic harbinger of change that greatly outweighed their actual numbers.”
272951dc-4e51-55bc-bf53-6fb35a332aa6.author: Cristina Mosillo, Giulia Barrera

2739eecb-f1a1-5544-8ead-dcf31ff17148.name: An elderly Paul Draneht (1815–94) with his daughter Despina
2739eecb-f1a1-5544-8ead-dcf31ff17148.short_description: In 1894, Paul Draneht, who had been awarded the title of Pasha, died in Alexandria. His daughter Despina married a Greek businessman, Emmanuel Zervudachi, and the family continued to be part of a Mediterranean cosmopolitan elite.

275443d0-1d7d-5e19-a7ef-50820f9add5d.name: *Convoy of pilgrims*
275443d0-1d7d-5e19-a7ef-50820f9add5d.short_description: The Hijaz Railway was a narrow-gauge railway (1,050mm/​3ft, 5 11⁄32 in track gauge) that ran from Damascus to Medina, through the Hijaz region of Saudi Arabia, with a branch line to Haifa on the Mediterranean Sea. It was a part of the Ottoman railway network and was built to extend the line from the Haydarpaşa Terminal in Istanbul beyond Damascus to the holy city of Mecca. It got no further than Medina, 400 kilometres (250mi) short of Mecca, due to the construction interruption caused by the outbreak of World War I. The main purpose of the railway was to establish a connection between Constantinople, the capital of the Ottoman Empire and the seat of the Islamic Caliphate, and Hijaz in Arabia, the site of the holiest shrines of Islam and the holy city of Mecca, the destination of the Hajj (annual pilgrimage).
275443d0-1d7d-5e19-a7ef-50820f9add5d.holder: Istanbul University, Nadir Eserler Kütüphanesi (Rare Books Library)

275bf73d-6170-5205-804c-fbb1ff637342.name: Yıldız Tile Imperial Factory
275bf73d-6170-5205-804c-fbb1ff637342.short_description: The Yıldız Tile Imperial Factory was founded by Sultan Abdülhamid II (1876-1909) in the early 1890’s in the garden of Yıldız Palace for the purposes of arousing, reshaping and stimulating the Turkish tiling art. The factory, which began manufacturing immediately, was damaged in the earthquake of 1894 and in the same year, it was nearly reconstructed by Italian Architect Raimondo d’Aronco.

27e660f6-6597-5bf6-8766-18aaf9b3ddc1.short_description: Petrie was a pioneer of archaeological photography, even though at the time the technique of half-toning had not been developed, so that his photographs had to be turned into woodcuts for publication. 28039875-4e38-5259-a55c-6b799bdfae9b.name: Grand Bazar Arabe. A late-19th-century bazaar built in Tunis by the construction company of G. Di Vittorio, an Italian immigrant in Tunisia
28039875-4e38-5259-a55c-6b799bdfae9b.short_description:
On the main entrance one can read the shop sign “Grand Bazar Kassar Said”; on the left “Grand Bazar Arab” and on the right, one can read the shop sign “I. Piperno”: Piperno is an unmistakably Italian Jewish name.  
Giuseppe Di Vittorio, who ran the construction company that built this building, migrated from Termini Imerese (a small town near Palermo, Sicily, Italy) in 1882.

2a8f3f10-1a76-54cb-bfe6-0ccb6a3700bd.name: Picture frame with photograph of James Camille Samson
2a8f3f10-1a76-54cb-bfe6-0ccb6a3700bd.short_description: Part of the decorum of upper class houses in the late 19th century was the convivial circle of gentlemen who retired to the smoking room after dinner to enjoy cognac, cigars and conversation while the hostess entertained her female guests with tea in the ladies’ salon. In the period of the World’s Fair and modern tourism, a tremendous stylistic diversity was available for decorating the smoking room. Moorish-Oriental styles were fashionable: heavy Persian carpets on the floors, Anatolian kilims on the walls, furniture plushily upholstered, side tables with mother-of-pearl inlays, palm plants and hookahs and Caucasian daggers. Trophies and souvenirs of journeys, including picture frames with ﬁnely turned *mashrabiya* latticework were mostly mass-produced in Europe and purchased in specialised furniture shops.

2df6225e-8ea7-5fef-a311-cc29307168e3.short_description: Of great importance for the collection of the first Museum of Islamic Art in the western world are the findings made during the excavations in Samarra, which were conducted by Ernst Herzfeld and the museum’s first director, Friedrich Sarre, between 1911 and 1913. 2f499780-f936-5142-8597-fc27d9b2d0ce.name: An old exhibition from Tiled Kiosk
2f499780-f936-5142-8597-fc27d9b2d0ce.short_description: The Tiled Kiosk is a pavilion set within the outer walls of Topkapı Palace and dates from 1472. It was built by the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II as a pleasure palace or kiosk. The building was used as the Imperial Museum between 1875 and 1891. In 1953, it was opened to the public as a museum of Turkish and Islamic art, and was later incorporated into the Istanbul Archaeology Museums. The collections of the Tiled Kiosk Museum consist of about 2000 artefacts belonging to the Seljuk and Ottoman eras, dating from the 11th-20th centuries. These artefacts include those that existed when the museum was incorporated into the İstanbul Archaeological Museums due to its closeness and those acquired through excavations, purchases, donations and confiscations.

307c3b5c-a525-55c7-89a1-8342e6da903a.name: Dolmabahçe Palace Imperial Gate
307c3b5c-a525-55c7-89a1-8342e6da903a.short_description: James Robertson arrived in Istanbul in 1840 and started work as head etcher in Ottoman Mint. He began taking photos of Istanbul soon after. Dolmabahçe Palace was built by Sultan Abdulmecid (1839-1861), who was the thirty first Ottoman Sultan. The palace, whose construction commenced on 13 June 1843, was brought into use on 7 June 1856, upon completion of its surrounding walls. The palace mainly consists of three parts: the Imperial Mabeyn (State Apartments), Muayede Salon (Ceremonial Hall) and the Imperial Harem. Evident Western influences, observed in the style, details and ornaments, are reflections of the aesthetic values as they changed through the last period of the Imperial. On the other hand, it is a building complex in which traditional Turkish House style was applied on a large scale with respect to spatial organization and the relationships between the rooms and salons.
keywords: Photograph; Old İstanbul Photograph; İstanbul; James Robertson

309c53a9-a0ef-5547-8426-cd89d2b38012.name: Istanbul Port
309c53a9-a0ef-5547-8426-cd89d2b38012.short_description: During the 19th century, new technologies radically transformed both travel and communications. The construction of Galata Pier began in 1892, and was completed in 1900. Two warehouses were built in 1910, and three more were added in 1928. From 1925 on, the port authority started to give all the necessary logistics support to the ships, including water and coal supply, loading and unloading, maritime pilotage and marine salvage services.

30cc5fa9-8b03-5f71-9493-92a9a15324e0.name: Migration preparations from Lemnos island to Turkey
30cc5fa9-8b03-5f71-9493-92a9a15324e0.short_description: The 1923 population exchange between Greece and Turkey was based upon religious identity, and involved the Greek Orthodox citizens of Turkey and the Muslim citizens of Greece. The "Convention Concerning the Exchange of Greek and Turkish Populations" was signed at Lausanne, Switzerland, on 30 January 1923, by the governments of Greece and Turkey. During the migration waves during the 1896-97 riots in Crete, 40,000 Cretan Muslims had to migrate to territories under Ottoman rule: Lebanon, Syria and Anatolia. This photograph pertains to migration preparations from Lemnos to Turkey in 1924.
30cc5fa9-8b03-5f71-9493-92a9a15324e0.holder: Population Exchange Museum (The Foundation of Lausanne Treaty Emigrants)
keywords: migration; population exchange

31671ff1-195a-54da-8c1f-6f9b776bf0e8.name: Statue of Cardinal Lavigerie
31671ff1-195a-54da-8c1f-6f9b776bf0e8.short_description: On the 23 November 1925, the French resident-general in Tunisia, Lucien Saint, organised a solemn gathering to commemorate 100 years since Cardinal Lavigerie's birth. The municipality of Tunis also received a statue of him brandishing a cross by the sculptor Élie-Jean Vézien, which they chose to put in Place Bab el-Bhar (at the entrance to the medina), a place of great importance to Tunisians. This choice of location angered the Tunisian population and triggered a protest from the students of the Zaytuna University, who considered this act an attack on their religious beliefs (it was placed close to the Zaytuna Mosque) and their traditions. The statue stayed there until Tunisian independence, when it was removed by the Mayor of Tunis.  Lavigerie was the Archbishop of Algiers and Carthage, and the founder of the Pères Blancs in 1868.
31671ff1-195a-54da-8c1f-6f9b776bf0e8.holder: Institut Supérieur d’Histoire Contemporaine de la Tunisie
31671ff1-195a-54da-8c1f-6f9b776bf0e8.author: Bechir Yazidi

32e505cb-9f9d-5883-b87d-e0aff2e6436e.name: Pera Palace Hotel
32e505cb-9f9d-5883-b87d-e0aff2e6436e.short_description: Pera Palace Hotel was built in 1892 for the purpose of hosting the passengers of the Orient Express and was named after its location. Alexander Vallaury, a French-Turkish architect living in the city designed the hotel in a blend of neo-classical, art nouveau and oriental styles. The hotel was the first building in Turkey to be powered by electricity other than the Ottoman Palaces. It was also the only address in the city to provide hot running water for its guests and was home to the first electric elevator in Istanbul.
32e505cb-9f9d-5883-b87d-e0aff2e6436e.holder: Istanbul University, Nadir Eserler Kütüphanesi (Rare Books Library)

33c78378-09b9-5e76-bb0d-85f0948fe81c.name: Inocencia Serrano y Cerver, Marquise of Cerralbo, and Amelia del Valle y Serrano, in Oriental garment
33c78378-09b9-5e76-bb0d-85f0948fe81c.description: The Marquis of Cerralbo and his family visited Istanbul in 1889, and nowadays the Cerralbo Museum holds an interesting variety of pieces bought and collected as souvenirs from the family trip. When visiting a foreign country or city, being portraited by a famous photographer of studio was indispensable. In this case the photographers are the world-renowned Armenian Abdullah Frères, Photographes de S. M. I. le Sultan. This albumen portrait of Inocencia Serrano y Cerver, Marquise of Cerralbo, and her daughter Amelia del Valle y Serrano is delicious thanks to the typical Turkish costume, the apparently easy pose and the scenography and the absolute harmony with the idea of aesthetic orientalism.
33c78378-09b9-5e76-bb0d-85f0948fe81c.author: Cecilia Casas Desantes
keywords: Portrait; women; souvenir; memorabilia; orientalism

3461e5ef-930c-5a8d-8393-eeb23e8eaffa.name: The female surgery division of the Italian hospital in Tunis
3461e5ef-930c-5a8d-8393-eeb23e8eaffa.short_description:
Prior to the establishment of the French protectorate on Tunisia in 1881, Italian doctors operated in Tunisia. The Bey had frequently employed Italian physicians. Some were born in Tunisia, of Jewish families from Livorno, others had arrived in Tunisia as political exiles in the first half of the 19th century. The largest contingent of Italian doctors, however, migrated to Tunisia after 1881.  
In 1890, the Italian community opened a hospital with about 100 beds. Italian physicians worked in the hospital as volunteers and indigent patients were treated for free. The initial funding for creating and running the hospital came from the Italian community; the Italian state contributed to pay the expenses for the construction of a new facility in 1900 and partly subsidized the hospital activities.
3461e5ef-930c-5a8d-8393-eeb23e8eaffa.author: Giulia Barrera

348adef4-1494-549d-bfba-21cff66740ba.short_description: A 19th photography focus  the hall of a bourgeois residence: at Barahona's Palace, in a rural city: Évora. This photo shows the bourgeois inside domestic glamour, with some influences of the luxury oriental palaces.

35118a9c-ae87-5875-b6fd-694c3a29ac01.name: *The Moroccan Embassy in Rome*
35118a9c-ae87-5875-b6fd-694c3a29ac01.short_description:
In June 1890, the Sultan of Morocco sent an Ambassador to Italy (Hagi El Maati el Mazamizi), to meet the Italian King and present him with gifts.  
The Ambassador was received with the highest honours. He met with the Italian Prime Minister and with the King, who offered him a gala dinner.  
In these pictures one can see (from the top left): four captains who escorted Morocco’s Ambassador, his interpreter Lamfaddal Elkabbagi, the Ambassador on a carriage arriving at the King’s palace, Hamed (one of the Ambassador’s servants), Pà Nadan (another servant), and two children travelling with the Ambassador on the hotel’s terrace.
35118a9c-ae87-5875-b6fd-694c3a29ac01.holder: State Library of Modern and Contemporary History
35118a9c-ae87-5875-b6fd-694c3a29ac01.author: Giulia Barrera

351cda3e-2855-5288-9f93-722ee2410530.name: Beykoz Pavilion
351cda3e-2855-5288-9f93-722ee2410530.short_description: The construction of Beykoz Pavilion began by order of Mehmed Ali Pahsa, Governor of Egypt in 1845 and upon his death was completed in 1854. The two-storeyed, half-timbered building has a symmetrical plan and neo-classical façade and designed as a hall in the middle with rooms surrounded. Photographs of the pavilion taken during the reign of Sultan Abdülhamid II reveal its rich decoration with gilded furniture, upholsteries and curtains of Hereke fabrics, Baccarat vases and large crystal chandeliers.
351cda3e-2855-5288-9f93-722ee2410530.holder: Istanbul University, Nadir Eserler Kütüphanesi (Rare Books Library)

351e4901-7c17-581f-9b15-8be1d6fc3458.name: Au Palais Arabe. A furniture shop of the Italians Eugenio and Alfredo Coen in Tunis
351e4901-7c17-581f-9b15-8be1d6fc3458.short_description: “Au Palais Arabe”, Rue de Rome, 3, Tunis, was once the most important shop in town for furniture and other household items. Eugenio Coen (born in Livorno in 1855, migrated to Tunis in 1885) and his brother Alfredo (born in Livorno in 1868 and migrated to Tunis in 1887) also ran a furniture factory that, in 1906, employed about 100 carpenters, cabinet makers and other workers, 80 per cent of whom were Italian.

355b8a63-ea50-5b91-9873-7e2c8152cab8.name: *Catholic mission to Brazzaville: Brazzaville mission school - Vive la France!*
355b8a63-ea50-5b91-9873-7e2c8152cab8.short_description: Evangelism and colonialism often went hand in hand, working together to Christianise local populations. The missionaries considered French society as the perfect model of Christian society, and the government thought missions would help consolidate colonialism. Schools were one of the places where this relationship is the most evident. This image clearly shows how the French instilled young African children with love for the French flag from a very young age.

363a9b8e-3ef5-567b-a032-97afeab68478.name: Trail from the village of Deir el-Medina to the Valley of the Queens
363a9b8e-3ef5-567b-a032-97afeab68478.short_description: This photograph was taken by an unknown author during the excavations led by Ernesto Schiaparelli in Egypt. Schiaparelli (1856-1928) was Director of the Egyptian Museum of Florence from 1881 to 1894 and in 1894 became Director of the Egyptian Museum of Turin. The photograph shows a section of a trail in the south of Deir el-Bahri. It is easy to recognize the ruins of a residential district, which presumably hosted the workers and the artisans involved in the works for the tombs of the Valley of the Queens. Ernesto Schiaparelli, first as museum director and then as excavation superintendent from 1907 to his death, led several excavation campaigns around 1903-1914 in the Valley of the Queens, a place dedicated to the burial of wives, princes and princesses since the reign of Rameses I.

36d58a55-2db8-5fb1-a95f-93e3fa5513d2.name: Ottoman Clothing Album
36d58a55-2db8-5fb1-a95f-93e3fa5513d2.short_description: With the political developments of the 19th century, interest in the East increased steadily in the western world. Everything belonging to the East was the centre of interest for western observers. As a result, close to 160 artists visited Istanbul in the 19th century. Pascal Sébah (1823-86) was a pioneer photographer who worked in Istanbul. Sébah opened a photography studio known as "El Chark " in Pera in 1857. The studio's most successful period started with the Vienna Universal Exhibition in 1873. Sébah formed a partnership with Joaillier Polycarpe in 1885. In 1899, the two partners bought Abdullah Frères's archives. For the Vienna Universal Exhibition in 1873, Pascal Sébah prepared *The Ottoman Clothing Album* to be exhibited at the Ottoman Stand.

3879757a-f06b-5c78-885b-5bf3ddf848b8.name: *Convoy of pilgrims*
3879757a-f06b-5c78-885b-5bf3ddf848b8.short_description: The Hijaz Railway was a narrow-gauge railway (1,050mm/​3ft, 5 11⁄32 in track gauge) that ran from Damascus to Medina, through the Hijaz region of Saudi Arabia, with a branch line to Haifa on the Mediterranean Sea. It was a part of the Ottoman railway network and was built to extend the line from the Haydarpaşa Terminal in Istanbul beyond Damascus to the holy city of Mecca. It got no further than Medina, 400 kilometres (250mi) short of Mecca, due to the construction interruption caused by the outbreak of World War I. The main purpose of the railway was to establish a connection between Constantinople, the capital of the Ottoman Empire and the seat of the Islamic Caliphate, and Hijaz in Arabia, the site of the holiest shrines of Islam and the holy city of Mecca, the destination of the Hajj (annual pilgrimage).

39343989-0847-535d-82c3-ecbf42c6b4d6.name: Valley of the Queens, Tomb of Prince Khaemwaset at the moment of discovery
39343989-0847-535d-82c3-ecbf42c6b4d6.short_description: Francesco Ballerini was an archaeologist and a curator of the Egyptian Museum in Turin. He worked at the 1902 Italian Archaeological Mission in Egypt led by Ernesto Schiaparelli. He also took part in four other excavations including the tombs of Khaemuaset (No. 44) and Sethherkhepeshef (No. 43), both sons of the Pharaoh Rameses III (1183–1152 BC). The tombs were found cluttered with wooden sarcophagi and mummies dating back to a period between the 22nd-25th dynasties, as the picture shows. Both tombs had been robbed previously and showed the pink granite sarcophagi already opened and empty. In the background the viewer can see the scene of the triumph of Osiris, God of the Afterworld. The God is flanked by two funeral genii, guardians of the gates to the afterworld.

3a9203b3-ee28-58a5-9738-28760f62fc9b.name: Photograph
3a9203b3-ee28-58a5-9738-28760f62fc9b.short_description:
This photograph is taken from a family photograph album. Most of the photographs in it are printed on platinum paper, which was introduced in 1879.  
Throughout most of the 19th century women had few legal rights to property, money, children, or even, after marriage, their own bodies. However, there were great changes in attitudes during the last decade of the century. The traditional role of women was questioned and some women openly defied convention. They educated themselves by reading widely and took up what were seen as 'un-ladylike' activities such as smoking and cycling. The free movement of the bicycle was seen as a symbol of equality and personal freedom.

3abe2459-c22d-5b5d-907a-4be0147c9eec.name: Seated Berber woman (Nailiya)
3abe2459-c22d-5b5d-907a-4be0147c9eec.description:
The image depicts a Nailiya, a woman of the Berber tribe of the Ouled Naïl, in the south of Algeria. She is sitting among rich cushions, wearing a colourful silk dress and the jewels used to perform their traditional dance.  
The Nailiyat were independent women, free to marry men of their choosing. They moved to the cities in the North to earn money as dancers, in order to maintain their families in their community of origin. All this was not fully understood by Europeans. With the emergence of sex tourism these women were forced to introduce sexual content in their originally hieratic performance, and finally they were even considered as prostitutes by the French administration, in turn leading to being repudiated in their villages.  
Early photography contributed to forge this image of the Nailiyat in the European imagination.
keywords: Photography; Orientalism; Algeria; Women

3ae243ba-330f-5d5a-a7ac-1134d23470a9.name: The Ottoman Bank
3ae243ba-330f-5d5a-a7ac-1134d23470a9.short_description: One of the world's largest photo archives, Abdülhamid II's photo archives – knows as the Yildiz Albums – contain about 37 thousand pictures from that period of the Ottoman Empire. The photo archives contain images of cities, buildings which were built by sultan, schools, students, soldiers, mosques, ports, government departments, shipyards, railways, bridges, bazaars, machines, locomotives and factories. The Ottoman Bank was founded in 1856 in the Galata business section of Istanbul, the capital of the Ottoman Empire, as a joint venture between British interests, the Banque de Paris et des Pays-Bas of France, and the Ottoman government. *Tanzimat* era's principal renovations in the financial field were the reestablishment of the currency and the foundation of the Ottoman Bank.
3ae243ba-330f-5d5a-a7ac-1134d23470a9.holder: Istanbul University, Nadir Eserler Kütüphanesi (Rare Books Library)

3b50b4cf-8492-533e-8f06-4e7806420158.short_description: Alix de Hesse-Darmstadt, who became the last Empress of Russia under the name Alexandra Romanova, was the granddaughter of none other than Queen Victoria of England. Nikolai II and his wife Alexandra stopped off in England on the way to Paris for their official trip in 1896, to introduce their first child (Olga) to her great-grandmother, Queen Victoria.  This photo is more of a family portrait than an official image.

3bc61cff-a133-5a4c-8c91-17c972723305.name: Winston Churchill waving his hat atop his walking stick in front of the Zunfthaus zur Meisen
3bc61cff-a133-5a4c-8c91-17c972723305.description:
Winston Churchill waves to a cheering crowd packed into the cathedral square in Zurich after giving a speech on 19 January 1946. Churchill visited Switzerland again from 23 August to 20 September 1946 when he travelled from Geneva via Lausanne and Bern to Zurich where he gave his famous speech on Europe at the University of Zurich. Although by then he was leader of the opposition, and was on a private visit to Switzerland, Churchill received an enthusiastic welcome befitting a statesman.  
Everywhere he went, photographers treated Churchill’s trip through Switzerland like a state visit. The Presse Diffusion Lausanne (PDL) agency covered his visits to Lausanne and Zurich. The Swiss National Museum acquired the archives of PDL and Actualités Suisses Lausanne (ASL) in 2007. Combined they number around six million images in the form of negatives, prints, and slides. Covering the years from 1937 to 1999, they record the most significant developments during the era of analogue press photography.
3bc61cff-a133-5a4c-8c91-17c972723305.method_for_datation: Documents. The year and place of production were written on the paper-envelopes that contained the negatives in the archives
3bc61cff-a133-5a4c-8c91-17c972723305.obtention: The ASL and PDL archives were bought in 2007
keywords: Photography; Press Photography; Actualités Suisse Lausanne; Presse Diffusion Lausanne; Winston Churchill; Zuerich; Zunfthaus zur Meisen; Speech
materials: Gelatin silver film, medium format negative, flexible film carrier

3dcfae1b-7081-54c3-beee-e83c87032c40.name: Photograph - Masjid Al Haram Flooding
3dcfae1b-7081-54c3-beee-e83c87032c40.short_description:
This photograph documents the flood of the Masjid Al Haram in Mecca after the heavy rainfall in 1952. Captured at the centre of the photograph is the Kaaba, surrounded by the mosque *Masjid Al Haram*, with its minarets stretching across the background.  
Mecca and the Kaaba have witnessed several floods throughout history, including the years 1941, 1913, and long before in 1727 and 1728. Inundations have sadly weakened the internal architecture.  
During Hajj, the Muslim pilgrimage and one of Islam's pillars, observants perform Tawaf, the circumambulation around the Kaaba for a repeated number of times. Rare instances of worshippers performing Tawaf by swimming have been recorded. Among these are Abd Allah al-Zubayr, a companion of Prophet Muhammad (PBUH).
