afe3b20f-d59e-5494-b4ec-e5a4b9544ad9.short_description: Zeybek is a folk dance from Western Anatolia. It is done either by one or several dancers moving in a circle. Zeybek represents the protector. The dancer keeps his arms upright on the shoulder level while sometimes they are curled from elbow. He moves slowly with long steps. From time to time he kneels to touch his knee down.

b0404c66-90f7-54a0-8b0e-c5174cdc9947.name: Liban. Jamhour. La gare. (Jamhour Station, Lebanon)
b0404c66-90f7-54a0-8b0e-c5174cdc9947.description: Jamhour Station was an intermediate stop on the Beirut–Damascus railway, situated on the ascent from Beirut through Mount Lebanon between Baabda and Chouit–Araya stations. Located approximately twelve kilometres from the Beirut terminus and around 380 metres above sea level, Jamhour formed part of the railway's rapid climb from the Mediterranean coast toward the highest station of Dahr el Baidar, 1487 metres above sea level.

b09ea51a-72ba-5a0c-8a5d-88c708d9a1fa.name: Women going about their daily life
b09ea51a-72ba-5a0c-8a5d-88c708d9a1fa.short_description: In the eary 20th century the Tunisian woman, like her counterparts around the world, led a difficult life of hard work and exclusion from public life which was considered a man's world. Although it is important to take into account the variety of women's circumstances and experiences, depending on their background, it was nonetheless rare for a Tunisian woman at this time to have access to religious sciences, Arabic literature and even less so to the physical and mathematical sciences. The era of the great female poets, litterateurs and arts advocates in Kairouan had long passed. However a debate surrounding women's education was opening up in Tunisia, and particularly in Egypt, which presented women's education as a essential to the emancipation of society.

b1761f2e-80b8-586f-b4e2-c3736d979725.name: Photograph of an employee outside the *Poste-Cherifienne* office
b1761f2e-80b8-586f-b4e2-c3736d979725.description: The first national post and transport service in Morocco was founded by Mulay al-Hasan I on 20 Jumada I 1390 (22 November 1892) and was known as the *Poste-Makhzen*. The office was established in order to take control nationally of the postal (mainly parcels and messengers) service in Morocco, but competition from private foreign firms was tough. When in 1892 the Sultan first gave orders for port managers to take control of Morocco’s interests in this regard, this nascent organisation included 13 Moroccan cities, defined as zones connected by transport links, and each defined by specific costs.

b1ada77d-4a0f-5105-a292-423509ecec6b.name: Haydarpaşa Train Station
b1ada77d-4a0f-5105-a292-423509ecec6b.short_description: In 1871 Sultan Abdülaziz ordered a rail line to be built from Haydarpaşa to İzmit. Haydarpaşa station opened in 1872, and in 1888 the Anatolian Railway (CFOA) took over the line and the station. Since the station was built next to the Bosporus, freight trains would unload at Haydarpaşa and the freight would be transferred to ships. Haydarpaşa was chosen to be the northern terminus of the Baghdad Railway and the Hijaz Railway in 1904 and with rail traffic increasing, a new and larger building was required. The Anatolian Railway hired two German architects; Otto Ritter and Helmut Conu to build the new building. They chose a neo-classical structure and construction started in 1906.

b20d222f-63fe-50b9-acfd-a854de63e772.name: Photograph: *A Mohammedan Funeral, Egypt*
b20d222f-63fe-50b9-acfd-a854de63e772.description: Stereoscopic photography that creates the illusion of depth of field from a two-dimensional image by using a specific viewfinder, or stereoscope. The photograph is formed by two apparently identical images mounted on a rigid board. Stereographic cards turned into a popular entertainment medium from the late 1880s until 1970, reaching its peak of popularity in the first decade of the twentieth century. The ceremonies of funeral, studied for example by the British anthropologist Edward William Lane around the time of the dating of the photography, are very similar for men and women: the wailing is produced by the family and community, and is accompanied by a series of prayers from the Qur´an and ritual cleansing of the body. In this photography, within this "farewell ceremony" we can distinguish the coffin and the funeral procession, mostly male, who plays different songs and prayers; after the coffin, the procession would be closed for the mourners.
keywords: Photography; funeral; ritual; travel; Egypt; scenes of life

b5eeac6a-d016-5d9a-8a53-0fd0bd897372.name: Excavation of l'Avenue de l'Opéra and Boulevard Henri IV
b5eeac6a-d016-5d9a-8a53-0fd0bd897372.short_description: When Napoléon III wanted a new opera house to be built (l’Opéra Garnier), he asked Haussmann to excavate the road beneath it, allowing him to go to the opera safely and without risk of being attacked from his residence at the Château des Tuileries. Haussman was forced to dig through an old neighbourhood, built on a hill. This photograph indicates the vastness of the works. The architect Garnier ordered Haussman to ensure no trees blocked the view of the opera house.
keywords: Haussmannisation; cities; Paris

b623eb8c-a4d4-585a-b9d5-23a452054f55.name: *Egypt, San. View of the excavations.*
b623eb8c-a4d4-585a-b9d5-23a452054f55.short_description: Emmanuel de Rougé was a French egyptologist who continued the work of Champollion. He was a member of l'Academie des Sciences, the curator of the "Musée Égyptien" of the Musée du Louvre (1849), professor of Egyptian archaeology at the Collège de France (1864), and authored many works on the history of Egypt. In 1862, he was sent on a mission to Egypt where he travelled along the Nile from the Delta to the cataracts, on a boat which had been loaned to the mission by Isma'il Pasha. This mission was the subject of a report and an illustrated publication with photographs by the Viscount Aymard de Banville. This photograph was taken at San, also known as the ancient site of Tanis, where the archaeologist Mariette was directing an excavation.
keywords: Egypt; archaeological mission; Egyptian antiquities.

b72b1d9c-a54e-5011-9c5b-63ebd9004f3a.name: Portrait of two ‘spahis’ from the French Army interned in Estavayer-le-Lac (FR)
b72b1d9c-a54e-5011-9c5b-63ebd9004f3a.description: This portrait from late 1940 / early 1941 shows two “spahi”, probably from the Seventh Algerian Spahi Regiment, interned in Estavayer-le-Lac. This “spahi” regiment was part of the second mounted brigade of the 45th French army corps that fought a hard rearguard action as German tank units drove French forces into the Jura Mountains in June 1940. At the request of General Marius Daille, the French forces were granted asylum in Switzerland. During WWII, Swiss press photographers of necessity turned their attention to events at home. In the context of the “national spiritual defence” policy, many features were produced in which Switzerland was shown turned in upon itself, getting on with everyday life at a remove from the war going on around it. Interned soldiers represented one of the few real points of contact the Swiss had with the war. The North African cavalry in their unusual uniforms were a real attraction and proved a popular subject for a grateful Swiss press corps, and the photographer from the Presse Diffusion Lausanne (PDL) agency. The Swiss National Museum acquired the archives of Actualités Suisses Lausanne (ASL) and Presse Diffusion Lausanne (PDL) in 2007. Combined they number around six million images in the form of negatives, prints, and slides. Covering the years from 1937 to 1999, they record the most significant developments during the era of analogue press photography.

b736daf3-734c-59a9-b14b-65272a0a6bc9.name: Stereoview entitled ‘*The Holy Carpet Parade, Cairo, Egypt- Starting for Mecca*’
b736daf3-734c-59a9-b14b-65272a0a6bc9.short_description: This very early photograph of the Mahmal ceremony, printed as a stereograph, shows the Mahmal parading through a narrow Cairene street amongst a thronging crowd; some bystanders have their arms outstretched in prayer. Behind travels a retinue of officials carrying banners, as the caravan leaves for pilgrimage. It was published by an American company based in Washington named J.F Jarvis, one of a small number of stereograph producers in the late 19th century. Jarvis began as a photographer using his own photographs to create stereographic views and later began publishing scenes from all over the world. This stereograph was sold by Underwood & Underwood. Founded in 1881 the company was known as the largest distributer of stereographs in the world until 1920, when it was sold to the Keystone View Company. Many of Underwood & Underwood’s stereographs depicted regions in the Middle East, covering landscapes and historical sites. This type of view may have originally been sold as part of a boxed set, together with other views of Egypt.

ba590c72-051f-5d9a-898f-073b4347852b.name: *Port, Beirut*
ba590c72-051f-5d9a-898f-073b4347852b.short_description: On 19/6/1887, the Ottoman authority gave the concession of the Port to an Ottoman company under the name of "Compagnie du Port, des Quais et des Entrepôts de Beyrouth". The concession was later fortified when the company gained from the Customs the sole rights to store and carry all the transit goods passing through the Customs. Constructions works namely a maritime dam to expand and develop the Port were accomplished and the opening on the occasion of the accomplishment of these works was celebrated by the end of 1894, basins were developed and spread between Ras Al Shamiah and Ras Al Mudawar. It forms the midpoint of three continents: Europe, Asia and Africa, which makes the Port a passage for ship fleets between East and West. During the mid 70's, the Port of Beirut was an important international trading station with the surrounding Arab countries and up until today it has preserved its commercial nature.

ba660d1c-5f38-5a9c-90c6-7a2cf5e424f9.name: Bau der Bagdadbahn (Baghdad Building)
ba660d1c-5f38-5a9c-90c6-7a2cf5e424f9.description: The Baghdad Railway was one of the largest railway projects in the late Ottoman Empire. The line was conceived as a continuation of the Anatolian railway system from Konya across southern Anatolia toward Baghdad. In 1903, a concession was made to the Imperial Ottoman Baghdad Railway Company, which planned to cross the Taurus Mountains, descend toward the Adana–Mersin line, and continue through Aleppo toward Mesopotamia. The mountainous sections created major engineering and financial difficulties. While the first 200 km from Konya to Bulgurlu opened in 1904, further construction slowed considerably, particularly because crossing the Taurus range required extensive tunnels, bridges and other infrastructure. The Baghdad Railway remained incomplete until 1940. The First World War interrupted the construction, and the dissolution of the Ottoman Empire left the project unfinished. The final section connecting the railway to Baghdad was later constructed by the Iraqi State between 1936 and 1940.

bca9a195-0769-5794-865b-e5e0b784277a.name: Italian police record of Romualdo Peppini (b. Turin 1863, d. Casablanca 1912), an Italian anarchist worker who immigrated to Morocco in 1901

Supporters of Italian unification, and especially the supporters of Republican nationalist ideologue Giuseppe Mazzini, were among the first migrants. After the Italian unification, some anarchists migrated, while under Fascism several antifascists took refuge in North Africa.

It was inaugurated during the time of King Faruq, the son of King Fu`ad, and houses a large number of collections related to agricultural and rural environments, as well as agricultural plants and animals.

bd41700c-08db-55d1-89a5-2d1602e75424.name: Welcoming Captives of Abdulhamid after the Constitution
bd41700c-08db-55d1-89a5-2d1602e75424.description: Beirut Port Station was a public gathering place during the political transformation of 1908. Its bilingual caption, “Welcoming Captives of Abdulhamid after the Constitution / Des emprisonnés bien accueillis de Abdulhamid après la Constitution,” identifies the crowd as welcoming prisoners associated with the rule of Sultan Abdülhamid II after the restoration of constitutional government. Abdülhamid II restored the Ottoman constitution and reconvened parliament after the Young Turk Revolution of July 1908, and it was accompanied by the release of political prisoners and exiles. Locally, there was relative public support for the constitutional revolution among sections of Beirut's intellectual and mercantile population.
bd41700c-08db-55d1-89a5-2d1602e75424.bibliography: Zhantiev, Dmitry, “Two Images of the Young Turk Revolution: Public Reaction in Beirut and Damascus to the Revolutionary Events of 1908 in the Ottoman Empire”, *Modern and Contemporary History*, 1 (2023).
keywords: Beirut; railway station; Young Turk Revolution; Station Constitution

bd511092-0183-5780-8a32-1842a109f127.name: Pictures from Palestine, Northern Arabia and the Sinai
bd511092-0183-5780-8a32-1842a109f127.description: Photographic account showing major sites and geographic features of Saudi Arabia, Jordan, Syria, Egypt, and Palestine. Pictures depict pilgrims on the Hajj to Mecca, Bedouins, the construction of the Hijaz Railway between Damascus and Medina, and views of Jeddah, Petra, and Mount Sinai. Most of the photographs were taken between 1905 and 1915 by Bernhard Moritz (1859–1939), a German Orientalist, Arabist, and archaeologist, but some also by his Turkish colleagues, especially for areas where non-Muslims were prohibited from going. From 1896 to 1911, Moritz headed the Khedival Library and Archive in Cairo, from where he conducted numerous research trips to the Sinai and Hijaz.
bd511092-0183-5780-8a32-1842a109f127.author: Giulia Martini
keywords: Railways; Saudi Arabia; Hejaz; Pilgrims and pilgrimages; Muslim; Saudi Arabia; Mecca; Scientific expeditions; Arab countries; Photomechanical reproductions

bd591c95-bb06-5105-b1bd-b95187ad7a88.name: Villa Maria, in Tunis, the mansion of Luigi Rey, the son of a migrant from Piedmont (Italy)
bd591c95-bb06-5105-b1bd-b95187ad7a88.short_description: Luigi Rey was the son of Italian immigrants Giuseppe Rey (1808-1897), of Piedmont and Adelaide Baldacci, of Tuscany. In 1836, Giuseppe Rey was dispatched to Tunis by his employer, a construction company from Genoa, to work in the Bardo Palace (the official residence of the Bey of Tunis). After completing the contract Giuseppe decided to stay in Tunisia, where he continued to work at the service of the Bey. Together with his three children (Luigi, Antonio and Pio), Giuseppe Rey set up a construction company that continued after his death. Predominantly with his brothers but at times on his own, Luigi Rey built a variety of private and public edifices, including the Tunisia Palace Hotel (designed by architect Resplandy).
bd591c95-bb06-5105-b1bd-b95187ad7a88.dates: Photograph: first years of the 20th century; building: late 19th century
bd591c95-bb06-5105-b1bd-b95187ad7a88.author: Giulia Barrera

bdc77deb-d803-5076-89a4-a826a7e730aa.name: The stand of the Italian Community in Tunisia at the International Exhibition held in Turin in 1911
bdc77deb-d803-5076-89a4-a826a7e730aa.short_description:
The picture shows how, on the occasion of the 1911 international exhibition in Turin the Italian community in Tunisia chose to represent itself by blending elements taken from the Italian and from the Tunisian material culture.  
One can read the sign E. & A. Coen, Tunisi, Susa, Sfax. Eugenio and Alfredo Coen were the owners of a furniture factory and of the imposing furniture shop, “Au Palais Arabe”, in downtown Tunis.
bdc77deb-d803-5076-89a4-a826a7e730aa.author: Massimo Sanacore, Giulia Barrera

be01848b-7ea6-50bc-b6b0-fc23630b1bfd.name: Casablanca: local inhabitants rebuilding their city
be01848b-7ea6-50bc-b6b0-fc23630b1bfd.short_description: Casablanca was host to many French architectural experiments, and became a model for urban planners worldwide. Marshall Hubert Lyautey called on Henri Prost (1874–1859) to direct architectural works in the French Protectorate of Morocco. Thus, Prost established new plans for the cities of Casablanca, Rabat, Fez, Meknes, and Marrakesh. He decided to build a "new French-style city" in Casablanca. This photograph shows the works at the junction between the old medina and the new quarter at the same height as the old clocktower, with a caption stressing the "Arab population's" contribution to the works.
keywords: Cities; urbanisation; colonies; Morocco; France

bf87a0de-3e3f-504b-8bbb-757c5d6c17a8.name: *Faculty of Medicine Sports Teams at the Egyptian University*
bf87a0de-3e3f-504b-8bbb-757c5d6c17a8.short_description: The first sports teams at Egyptian University's Faculty of Medicine, where students achieved many regional and international victories. The 1923 Constitution stipulated that “Primary education is mandatory for all Egyptian boys and girls”. A decree was issued for the establishment of a public university under the name “The Egyptian University” in 1925, comprised of four faculties; literature, science, medicine and law. Ever since its establishment, the University has paid great attention to sport and university sport teams.
keywords: Education; Students; Student Sports; Student Teams; Faculty of Medicine; Egyptian University

bfd5d0b7-c555-5670-8bef-67d8e0f7c0a2.name: Primary students at a village school in central Italy, which followed the teaching methods introduced by Maria Montessori
bfd5d0b7-c555-5670-8bef-67d8e0f7c0a2.short_description:
When Italy became a nation state in 1861, the illiteracy rate in the country was 78 per cent. In 1901, it was still at 56 per cent. Illiteracy was particularly high in the countryside. In 1877, the “Coppino Law”, made elementary schools mandatory and free of charge.  
Maria Montessori (1870-1952) was a medical doctor who developed innovative teaching methods for primary-school children. Her educational methods were first applied during the first decade of the 20th century. They met with great success and were applied in thousands of schools all over Europe and North America.
bfd5d0b7-c555-5670-8bef-67d8e0f7c0a2.author: Giulia Barrera

bff5b327-dd8c-55ac-a7f0-49d5bbc62548.name: *Works for the opening of the Corinth Canal*
bff5b327-dd8c-55ac-a7f0-49d5bbc62548.short_description:
The Corinth Canal under constuction, circa 1885. Photographer unknown.  
The Corinth Canal separates the Peloponnesian peninsula from the Greek. The idea of the canal was revived after Greece gained independence but soon abandoned due to economical reasons. The opening of the Suez Canal in 1869 gave an new impetus and the following year, the Zaimis government passed a law authorising the construction of the canal, which was formally inaugurated on 23 April 1882. Zaimis assigned the project to the Hungarian István Türr who set up the Société Internationale du Canal Maritime de Corinthe but the company failed and the project was finished by the company of Andeas Syngros. The canal was designed by the Hungarian engineer Béla Gerster with the assistance of the French Vincent Dauzants, a chief engineer of the Suez canal.
bff5b327-dd8c-55ac-a7f0-49d5bbc62548.author: Maria Dimitriadou
keywords: photo; Corinth

bfff2eb8-84d2-5740-8e2c-17b970a1f6dc.name: Photograph.
bfff2eb8-84d2-5740-8e2c-17b970a1f6dc.description: Sultan Süleyman the Magnificent (r. AH 926–73 / AD 1520–66) selected one of the hills of Constantinople on which to erect his mosque. Its prominent site above the surrounding buildings gives the characteristic silhouette of the town that can be seen from the far-off Asian side of the Golden Horn. That is the view usually preferred by photographers, stressing its architectural greatness and importance. Not so in the case of this photographer. He chose a different point of view on the mosque, a view from the southeast, which shows the back of the building. Although he focuses on the mosque, there is more. The building takes up the whole space from left to right of the picture. We can see the mosque and the typical arrangement of its domes. The four minarets tell us that there is a courtyard in front of it. But the mosque does not dominate the picture. It is shown as part of the urban structure communicating with the surrounding landscape. And we, the onlookers, are also part of the picture due to the skill of the photographer. He enables us, as if with the eyes of the mosque, to see the Bosphorus, the ships and the shore on the other side which is still little built on. In this way, the magnificence of the site and of the building is immediately transmitted to the onlooker. And a second point lets us become familiar with it. The photographer's view allows an intimate look at the tombs of the Sultan and his wife Hürrem behind the mosque. It is, therefore, not simply a building of the Sultan that we see; it is the mosque of Süleymaniye.
bfff2eb8-84d2-5740-8e2c-17b970a1f6dc.short_description: Photograph showing the mosque of Sultan Sulayman (AH 926–73 / AD 1520–66) in Constantinople. In the background, the silhouette of the town of the Asian side of the Golden Horn. In the foreground of the photograph, but behind the mosque, are the tombs of the sultan and his wife Haseki Hürrem.
bfff2eb8-84d2-5740-8e2c-17b970a1f6dc.method_for_datation: These kinds of photographs, bought as souvenirs mostly by Europeans, were very common during the second half of the 19th century. Wilhelmina von Hallwyl who bought the photograph for her collection travelled in 1901, so it must have been taken not too long before that date.
bfff2eb8-84d2-5740-8e2c-17b970a1f6dc.method_for_provenance: The photograph shows a building of Istanbul.
bfff2eb8-84d2-5740-8e2c-17b970a1f6dc.obtention: Bought by Wilhelmina von Hallwyl during her journey from Jerusalem to Istanbul in 1901. This photograph belongs to a collection of 2,364 photographs owned by the Hallwyl Museum from Morocco, Egypt, Palestine and Turkey covering a period from 1870 until 1927.
bfff2eb8-84d2-5740-8e2c-17b970a1f6dc.bibliography: Öztuncay, B., *The Photographers of Constantinople: Pioneers, Studios and Artists from 19th Century Istanbul*, Istanbul, 2003.
bfff2eb8-84d2-5740-8e2c-17b970a1f6dc.author: Friederike Voigt
keywords: Ottoman architecture

c007f06c-d190-5c7f-97a4-f7b8a6259c5a.name: *Palacete* \[small palace\], Avenida da República, Lisbon
c007f06c-d190-5c7f-97a4-f7b8a6259c5a.short_description: Avenida Ressano Garcia, a main residential area and development axe opens in the North of Lisbon, one of the “Avenidas Novas” plan. c2b70678-bfae-5de0-a210-547e266d7099.name: Emigrant family
c2b70678-bfae-5de0-a210-547e266d7099.short_description: The 1923 population exchange between Greece and Turkey was based upon religious identity, and involved the Greek Orthodox citizens of Turkey and the Muslim citizens of Greece. The "Convention Concerning the Exchange of Greek and Turkish Populations" was signed at Lausanne, Switzerland, on 30 January 1923, by the governments of Greece and Turkey. This photograph belongs to the Luka Likidis family, who migrated from Bodrum to Crete in 1916.

c2cc2d61-09ed-5140-86b6-7a7bc1706b32.name: Conversation with Nasser at the Royal Palace of Dedinje, Belgrade
c2cc2d61-09ed-5140-86b6-7a7bc1706b32.description: Josip Broz Tito and Gamal Abdel Nasser are shown in conversation at the Royal Palace of Dedinje in Belgrade on 16 July 1956, during Nasser's state visit to Yugoslavia. The two leaders, both in military uniform, appear relaxed and engaged, an image that also hints at their shared background as soldiers who became heads of state. The meeting came at a decisive moment in the search for a political alternative to the Cold War blocs. Two days later, Tito, Nasser and Indian Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru met on the Brioni Islands, where, on 19 July, they issued a joint statement articulating principles that would later become central to the Non-Aligned Movement, formally launched at the Belgrade Conference in 1961 with the participation of 25 countries. The photograph captures a moment in the deepening relationship between Yugoslavia and Egypt, at a time when states across Asia, Africa and beyond were seeking greater autonomy from the dominant Cold War blocs.

c30fb9aa-8248-5b4a-84f5-a4be2f553315.name: Oasis of Madkhal Meski
c30fb9aa-8248-5b4a-84f5-a4be2f553315.description: The subject of this image is 'The Blue Source' in the oasis of (Madkhal) Meski, near Er-Rachidia, in Morocco, distinguished by its expansive body of water encompassed by palm trees. This oasis is a paradigm of the urban landscape in desert regions, where water functions as a nexus for communities and urban life. It is enveloped by residential dwellings and commercial establishments.
c30fb9aa-8248-5b4a-84f5-a4be2f553315.author: Yelyzaveta Basysta
keywords: Water; Oasis; Madkhal Meski; Morocco.

c369fdd9-b766-5049-9f4f-a257d2df3d50.name: Rome Exhibition 1911 (Piazza d'Armi) – Sicilian Pavilion
c369fdd9-b766-5049-9f4f-a257d2df3d50.short_description: Within the International Exhibition of Rome in 1911 and related to the celebrations for the 50th anniversary of the Unification of Italy, a "Forum of Regions" was arranged in the Piazza d’Armi. The architect Ernesto Basile (1857–1932), author of the project for the Sicilian Pavilion, took inspiration from the Arab-Norman architecture in Sicily, in particular from Zisa Palace, the church of Saint John of the Hermits and the Cathedral of Monreale. On the outside, the building looked like a cube with plain walls decorated with blind pointed arches and battlements on top. Doors and windows show pointed arch as well. At the sides of the facades two small towers topped by a small small dome give to the palace a striking oriental look. On the inside, there was an open space with columns topped by capitals, walls decorated with mosaics and majolicas, and fountains.
c369fdd9-b766-5049-9f4f-a257d2df3d50.holder: Central Institute for Ethno-Anthropology, National Museum of Arts and Popular Traditions
c369fdd9-b766-5049-9f4f-a257d2df3d50.copyright: Copyright image: Roma, Istituto Centrale per la Demoetnoantropologia, ICDE, Archivio storico.
c369fdd9-b766-5049-9f4f-a257d2df3d50.author: Marina Minozzi
keywords: Universal exposition; Esposizione universale di Roma; exhibition building; exhibitions and urban spaces; model; reproduction; Modernism; Art Nouveau; Moorish style; Norman; San Giovanni degli Eremiti; Islamic art; Islamic influence; applied arts

c3b4eb2f-61ad-53f7-a9e3-79fafd0deca5.name: In the Steppe between Misrata and Zliten
c3b4eb2f-61ad-53f7-a9e3-79fafd0deca5.short_description: Italy and the Ottoman Empire signed a peace treaty that officially ended the Italo-Turkish war on October 18th, 1912, passing control of the former Ottoman provinces of Tripolitania, Fezzan, and Cyrenaica to Italy. The Ottoman army left Libya, but hostilities between Italian troops and the Arabs that did not acknowledge Italian authority continued. By July 1914, Italy was able to occupy almost all the territory of Tripolitania, the coast of Cyrenaica and part of the territory of Fezzan. In 1915 a great Arab insurrection broke out and forced Italy to abandon much of the territory it had previously occupied.
c3b4eb2f-61ad-53f7-a9e3-79fafd0deca5.holder: Italian Institute for African and Oriental Studies

c4179abe-6375-58e2-9109-f22b4b9e5ebd.name: Photograph: *Arabic School, Learning the Koran, Egypt*
c4179abe-6375-58e2-9109-f22b4b9e5ebd.description:
Stereoscopic photography that creates the illusion of depth of field from two apparently identical images mounted on a rigid board by using a specific viewfinder, or stereoscope.  
The arrival of Islam to Africa caused the birth of schools where the Qu'ran was taught in Arabic. Probably Islamic education was the first education system introduced in African populations. Islam establishes education as a key priority for children.  
Universities, *madrasas* (organised institutions with different levels for studying Islamic religion), and Qur'anic schools (first education that children receive) are used by Islam as educational institutions and have played an important role in spreading Islamic religious, social, moral and cultural values between African populations.  
In the *madrasas* and Qur'anic schools, the Qur'an is learned and memorised by reading and writing at a wooden table. The memorization of the Qur'an is done by copying the teacher a text written on paper, and later recited aloud until memorised. Students were not allowed to pass to another passage until the current passage had been memorized.
keywords: Photography; education; Egypt; scenes of life

c5b30d17-788f-5526-9443-d7a3c584472b.name: Italian peasants in Tunisia
c5b30d17-788f-5526-9443-d7a3c584472b.short_description: According to official statistics, in 1921 there were around 4,000 Italian peasants in Tunisia; together with their families they amounted to 15,400 people, or roughly 60 per cent of the Europeans employed in agriculture.

c5d1c4ee-c5dd-5526-a357-f968533cd6be.name: *Semiramis*
c5d1c4ee-c5dd-5526-a357-f968533cd6be.short_description: Staging of *Semiramis* in France, played in a set based on ancient sculptures. There is a mix of Egyptian and Assyrian costume, plus some fantasy.

c6e01d96-8a83-56ed-b3c1-ff2c1b9de353.name: A photograph showing the interior of Porto Municipal Museum
c6e01d96-8a83-56ed-b3c1-ff2c1b9de353.short_description: Creation of Allen Museum in Porto by João Francisco Allen, an Irish origin wealthy wine trader to exhibit his own collection. It was the first Portuguese museum opened to the public, albeit to a very limited way. The visitors were allowed only on Sunday (10.00-15.00), during weekdays the access to the collections was conditioned.

c7278b24-cf58-5191-9342-586e5560d4ff.name: *Mlle. Lauta, first* \[French\] *woman to get a degree in philosophy*
c7278b24-cf58-5191-9342-586e5560d4ff.short_description: Léontine Zanta (not Lauta, as indicated by the photograph) was the first French woman to receive a literature degree (not a philosophy degree), writing her thesis on revival of Stoicism in the 16th century. A journalist, teacher and novelist, she was also very interested in feminism.

c7423aea-5979-55f8-8902-e38b1ba58ec7.name: Photograph of a classroom at a traditional Qur'anic school
c7423aea-5979-55f8-8902-e38b1ba58ec7.description: In 1914, the French Protectorate put forward a new policy to modernise the education system in Morocco. Integrating the new policy with the traditional education system, scholars (the *'ulama´*) of al-Qarawiyyin University modernised educational material while still respecting the old system.

c783fc3a-6b1b-58c1-83a4-ba0e00d74936.short_description: Pictured here are schoolteacher teaching his young pupil to write.

c7de3940-ac44-5e99-93fd-416c7b6e83ea.name: Ihlamur Pavilion
c7de3940-ac44-5e99-93fd-416c7b6e83ea.short_description: The Ihlamur Pavilion is located at the intersection of Nüzhetiye Street between Ihlamur and Tesvikiye and has an area of about 25,000 square meters. The Ihlamur Pavilion consists of two kiosks: the Maiyet and Merasim Kiosk. The Merasim Kiosk was reserved for the sultan’s personal use. The Maiyet Kiosk, the simpler of the two, was used by the sultan’s entourage and family members, and it currently serves as a beautiful cafeteria. The kiosk is decorated with crystal chandeliers, European-style furniture, Hereke carpets, and decorated vases.
c7de3940-ac44-5e99-93fd-416c7b6e83ea.holder: Istanbul University, Nadir Eserler Kütüphanesi (Rare Books Library)

c7e1ed38-295a-5272-b536-f559755ccd2b.name: Photograph pitched wooden boats by the River Euphrates in Hit, Iraq
c7e1ed38-295a-5272-b536-f559755ccd2b.description:
This photograph, taken by explorer, archaeologist, writer, and colonial diplomat Gertrude Bell during her AH 1327 / AD 1909 travels in Mesopotamia, depicts traditional boats at shore beside the River Euphrates in Hit. The boats, which have been made using woven reeds, wood and bitumen, are one of many examples of traditional trade and craft captured within the Gertrude Bell Archive. The image was featured in Bell's AH 1329 / AD 1911 publication 'Amurath to Amurath', alongside many others taken during this trip.  
  
The photograph has been digitised using the original negative, which is held along with the original print in Bell's photograph album ('Album K'), within the Gertrude Bell Archive at Newcastle University Special Collections. It is contextualised by original diary entries and letters, also held within the Archive.
c7e1ed38-295a-5272-b536-f559755ccd2b.method_for_datation: Date and origin documented by Gertrude Bell, and confirmed by contextual material in Gertrude Bell Archive.
c7e1ed38-295a-5272-b536-f559755ccd2b.provenance: Photograph taken by Gertrude Bell in Hit, Iraq, during her AH 1327 / AD 1909 trip there, included in Photograph Album K, part of the Gertrude Bell Archive.
c7e1ed38-295a-5272-b536-f559755ccd2b.bibliography:
Bell, G. L., *Amurath to Amurath*, London: William Heinemann MCMXI, 1911: Fig. 61, pp.104-114.  
  
The Gertrude Bell Archive, Newcastle University. Available at: https://gertrudebell.ncl.ac.uk/.
c7e1ed38-295a-5272-b536-f559755ccd2b.author: Valentina Flex
keywords: Iraq; Mesopotamia; boats; reeds; bitumen

c7f58b8f-d101-5a99-a3cc-dcb898bbfeeb.name: An Algerian woman grinds her meal in an old wooden mill
c7f58b8f-d101-5a99-a3cc-dcb898bbfeeb.short_description: Many Western photographers took great interest in women's daily lives, or in daily rural tasks. In this photograph from 1920 an Algerian woman is pictured as she grinds wheat with a wooden pestle and mortar.

c833e26b-92ab-57d3-b0cc-19ebfd4b94d8.name: Souvenir of Khartoum and Egyptian Sudan
c833e26b-92ab-57d3-b0cc-19ebfd4b94d8.short_description: As photography became more widespread tourists began creating their own photo albums. In this English album of souvenirs, this photo of the chief of the Jewellers Trade Association of Khartoum (Sudan) is accompanied by a flattering commentary on his skill in decorating tea cups.
keywords: travelling; souvenirs; photographs; Egypt; Sudan

c88e4cac-7c3a-5acf-8cad-3a3c6bf1777f.name: Photograph: *Music School, Syria*
c88e4cac-7c3a-5acf-8cad-3a3c6bf1777f.description:
Stereoscopic photography that creates the illusion of depth of field from two apparently identical images mounted on a rigid board by using a specific viewfinder, or stereoscope.  
The images taken by the Keystone View Company show very different scenes related to lifestyles and traditions of different continents. In this case, there is a man playing a stringed instrument with a bow, possibly a type of rebec, surrounded by a group of children and two adults, who watch and listen carefully. In Syria, as in many other parts of the world, music has had and still has an important role as a means of transmitting knowledge and to celebrate individual and collective events, and is closely linked to rites, institutions, cultural and ideological activities of different humans. This image illustrates not only the practice of this activity, music, but also the transfer of knowledge from one generation to another; music serves as a vehicle of expression and relationship between members of a society.
keywords: Photography; music; Syria; scenes of life

c95dc265-e63b-5039-8f8f-a2652ee2dcba.name: Tripolitania (Libya). Italian soldiers in front of a Roman mosaic
c95dc265-e63b-5039-8f8f-a2652ee2dcba.short_description:
Italian soldiers in front of a Roman mosaic in Tripolitania, Libya. At their feet, almost at the centre of the photo, a plaque explains that: “These wonderful remains of Ancient Rome art and civilization” have been brought back to the admiration of posterity by the Italian soldiers of the Bersaglieri 33rd Battalion in 1911 and they “confirm… Italy’s right to rule over Tripolitania”.  
The plaque explicitly claims that Italy colonial ambitions over Libya were legitimate because Ancient Rome had once ruled over that territory. This line of argument was often used by Italian colonialists in order to legitimize Italian colonial ambitions over Libya.
c95dc265-e63b-5039-8f8f-a2652ee2dcba.holder: Central Institute for Cataloguing and Documentation (ICCD)
c95dc265-e63b-5039-8f8f-a2652ee2dcba.author: Giulia Barrera

ca84a358-0e08-5345-bc08-43570cf84e04.name: *Women grinding corn in Sinai*
ca84a358-0e08-5345-bc08-43570cf84e04.short_description: Many of the most popular subjects of stereographs were of topographical views or of scenes unfamiliar to the western audience for whom they were generally produced. This group of Islamic women from Egypt's Sinai Peninsula is shown grinding corn. Their faces are hidden by veils. The veil turns away the gaze while at the same time attracting it. The secrecy of the veil prompted fascination for what was often seen as the mysterious and exotic world of the East or the 'Orient' to 19th-century western viewers. In contrast, the men in the background confront the camera.

keywords: Women; stereograph; stereoscope; agriculture; peasants; work; Egypt; Sinai; grain; grinder; topography; photographs

cb52291b-7b0d-5472-b972-2e4f32848e2f.name: Recreating Assyria
cb52291b-7b0d-5472-b972-2e4f32848e2f.short_description: Early stereoview of the Assyrian Court at the Crystal Palace. Based on recent discoveries by Layard, who wrote the guidebook.

cb597bd9-06a6-5ba9-b5db-5eea1c140fcc.name: The disembarking of the first railway car in Libya
cb597bd9-06a6-5ba9-b5db-5eea1c140fcc.short_description: The railway in a colonial context was much more than a means of transport: it was a powerful symbol of modernity, of technological superiority of the colonisers over the colonised, and of mastery over the territory. In Libya, the Italians started building railroads from the first months of colonial rule. The first lines, inaugurated in 1912, connected Tripoli with Ain Zara (11 kms) and to Zanzur (39 kms). By the end of 1915, the railway lines in Libya amounted to 180 kilometres.
cb597bd9-06a6-5ba9-b5db-5eea1c140fcc.holder: Italian Institute for African and Oriental Studies
cb597bd9-06a6-5ba9-b5db-5eea1c140fcc.author: Giulia Barrera

cbdc629e-10f9-51ce-82d1-89858dea84f0.name: Munchar - arrival of the post
cbdc629e-10f9-51ce-82d1-89858dea84f0.short_description: French agriculture in Tunisia began either through the establishment of large properties by private initiatives, or the introduction of settlers by the public authorities. This is a photograph from the "first phase" - one of the "companies" (of "French farms") had purchased a large plot of land, and employed a number of (largely Arab and Italian) workers to cultivate it. Pictured is a local driver bringing the mail van to the immigrant communities in Munchar (in the Béja region.) This picture was taken to reassure prospective immigrants that they would be able to easily communicate with their families back home.

cbffe8c2-7457-5662-8cc7-208d2edc343c.name: The English Consulate (Ruins)
cbffe8c2-7457-5662-8cc7-208d2edc343c.short_description:
The author of this picture, Luigi Fiorillo, was an Italian photographer who migrated to Alexandria (Egypt) around 1870 and opened a successful photography shop. In 1877, he participated as photographer in an expedition to Shewa region (Ethiopia), organised by the Italian Geographical Society, and ten years later in an Italian military expedition for the colonial conquest of Eritrea.  
In 1882, Fiorillo was one of the few Europeans who remained in Alexandria after the anti-foreign rioting and documented the consequences of the British bombardment on Alexandria of July 11th. He collected 50 pictures of the city ruins in an album titled “Souvenir d'Alexandrie: Ruines, 1882”.  
On the back of some photos that he took in the 1880s, Fiorillo defines himself as “le photographe de Son Altesse le Prince Mohammed Toussoun Pasha” (the photographer of his Majesty Prince Mohammed Toussoun Pasha). Luigi Fiorillo died in 1898.
cbffe8c2-7457-5662-8cc7-208d2edc343c.author: Giulia Barrera

ce2e2bbf-52d8-50a7-83d7-5ee68152c911.name: \[The clown\] *"Chocolat" entertaining children at the hospital*
ce2e2bbf-52d8-50a7-83d7-5ee68152c911.short_description: Rafael Padilla (1868–1917) was born to an African family and sent to Cuba as a slave, where he was bought by a farmer from Bilbao. Once in Paris, he performed as a duo with Footit for twenty years. They drew their success from the contrast between the bad-tempered white clown and his punch-bag in the form of a black clown named "Chocolat", which left parisians, still unaccustomed to difference, in hysterics.

He contributed to the standardization of the modern Macedonian language, having given responses to some important issues of the history, culture and language of Macedonians.

d04ab320-9a12-53d1-93fd-cefc444af612.name: Italian postcard of colonial propaganda: 'The Turco-Italian War. The Italian governor taking possession of Tripoli'
d04ab320-9a12-53d1-93fd-cefc444af612.short_description:
In this postcard we see the first Italian public ceremony during the colonial conquest of Libya.  
As Terence Ranger pointed out in his essay “The invention of tradition in colonial Africa” in E. Hobsbawn and T Ranger, *The Invention of Tradition* (Cambridge University Press 1983), public ceremonies were a tool that was much used by colonial powers. Their goal was to grant a public image of legitimacy to colonial domination. In other words, colonial pomp and circumstance were intended to convey to colonial subject a notion of might and “prestige” of the colonisers.
d04ab320-9a12-53d1-93fd-cefc444af612.holder: State Library of Modern and Contemporary History
d04ab320-9a12-53d1-93fd-cefc444af612.author: Maria Pia Critelli, Giulia Barrera

d0827146-e2b8-5b30-8059-2505a64042be.short_description:

d0a848cc-445a-5603-a7fc-832f779a1817.name: Postcard of “Mecca-Pilger in der Eisenbahn, Jerusalem“. (Mecca-Pilgrims on the Railway)
d0a848cc-445a-5603-a7fc-832f779a1817.description: The photograph shows three passengers through the open windows of a wooden railway carriage on their journey to the annual Hajj, one of the largest recurrent pilgrimage movements of people in the Islamic world. Before the construction of the Hijaz Railway, pilgrims travelling toward the Holy Cities usually spent several weeks crossing many regions by walking and camel caravans. The opening of the railway between 1900 and 1908 reduced this journey to only a few days, making the pilgrimage faster, safer and more accessible for many travellers. At the same time, railway travel transformed the social experience of the pilgrimage. Shared railway carriages brought together pilgrims from different provinces, languages and social backgrounds, replacing much of the traditional rhythm of caravan travel with a new form of collective mobility that reflected the technological and administrative reforms in the late Ottoman period.
d0a848cc-445a-5603-a7fc-832f779a1817.bibliography: Petersen, Andrew, et al., *The Medieval and Ottoman Hajj Route in Jordan: An Archaeological and Historical Study*, Oxford: Oxbow Books, 2012.
keywords: Hijaz Railway; Hajj; pilgrimage; passenger carriage; Mecca; Medina; Jerusalem

d12751a5-ab84-5160-b99b-ce28227573a2.name: The embroiderers of Dar al-Kiswa in Cairo
d12751a5-ab84-5160-b99b-ce28227573a2.short_description:
Dar al-Kiswa started life as *warshat al-kharanfash* – a large factory established by Muhammad ‘Ali Pasha in 1817 in Cairo. 4000 young men from Cairo were assembled to work there as apprentices in a variety of crafts and trades. But by the 1880s, it had become a workshop dedicated to the production of the Meccan textiles. The workshop was closed down in the late 1990s.  
  
At its heyday, up to a hundred weavers, artisans and embroiderers were known to have worked in Dar al-Kiswa. One section of the workshop, the *qism al-zarkasha*, was responsible for embroidering the textiles that were sent to Mecca every year. Many were members of the same family and often started work there as young boys, remaining until they retired. In the 1930s thre were at least 60 there, with an average age of about 65.  
  
The photographs are of some of the employees working in the embroidery section at Dar al-Kiswa. It is not known when they were assembled, but it is likely to have been sometime around the 1940s–early 50s.
d12751a5-ab84-5160-b99b-ce28227573a2.holder: Khalili Family Trust – Hajj and the Arts of Pilgrimage Collection
d12751a5-ab84-5160-b99b-ce28227573a2.bibliography: Nassar, N., “Dar al-Kiswa al-Sharifa. Administration and Production”, in Porter, V., and Saif, L. (eds), *The Hajj: Collected Essays*, London: British Museum, 2013: 175–83.
d12751a5-ab84-5160-b99b-ce28227573a2.author: Nahla Nassar
keywords: Calligraphy; Ceremonial object; Cotton; Curtain; Embroidery; Hajj; Hijaz; ka'ba; Minbar; Ottoman textile; Pilgrimage; Pilgrimage route; Religion; Religious object; Silk; Silver; Textile; Travel; Mecca

d2293b15-b277-5cf9-b55b-a5c86bba494e.name: Waterway in Nizwa, Oman
d2293b15-b277-5cf9-b55b-a5c86bba494e.description: The *aflaj* (singular *falaj*) are one of the oldest irrigation systems still in use today. Its origins date back to 5,000 years ago, though the example here is from AD 500. Its channels convey water from underground sources, springs and stream flow to villages and towns all around Oman. This system is employed as a primary water source for agricultural and domestic purposes, accounting for more than 30% of water usage across Oman. Using gravity forces to maintain the flux of water and its distribution, it has emerged as a distinguished social, cultural and economic emblem of the Omani landscape. The responsibility for the maintenance of working falaj and the distribution of water to different settlements lies with these communities. Despite the existence of numerous wells that provide potable water, the presence of aflaj waterways is of pivotal significance to the agricultural prosperity of Oman. The Falaj Daris, seen here, are the largest of the aflaj in Oman, and played a big part in Nizwa’s former prosperity as the capital of Oman in the 6th and 7th centuries AD. In 2006, the Aflaj Irrigation System was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site and consequently granted governmental protection.
d2293b15-b277-5cf9-b55b-a5c86bba494e.author: Yelyzaveta Basysta
keywords: Water; aflaj; irrigation systems.

d4c7f9c0-dc66-5391-8685-09943014060f.name: Gjorche Petrov
d4c7f9c0-dc66-5391-8685-09943014060f.short_description: Gjorche Petrov (1865–1921) was a prominent member of the Internal Macedonian Revolutionary Organization (VMRO). He was born in Prilep on 2 March 1865. He obtained his elementary education in his native town and attended gymnasium in present day Bulgaria. He worked as a teacher in several Macedonian towns. He worked out, together with Gotze Delchev, the Statute of VMRO. The aim of the organization clearly expressed in Article 1 of the Statute was attaining full political autonomy of Macedonia and the Adrianopole Region. The structure of the organization was also defined as consisting of village, regional and district committees and lead by the Central Committee. Becoming one of the leaders of the Internal Macedonian Revolutionary Organization he shared Gotze Delchev’s conviction that the uprising was not supposed to begin before all regions in Macedonia were fully prepared for it in terms of training of the troops and providing arms.
d4c7f9c0-dc66-5391-8685-09943014060f.author: Nada Andonovska (author), Dragan Georgiev, historian (consultant)

d571791c-a497-50be-b648-cbb508ceae8f.name: Manifestation celebrating King Fu`ad I
d571791c-a497-50be-b648-cbb508ceae8f.short_description: Fayum Directorate Arabs at the reception of King Fu`ad I. Fu`ad I ruled Egypt from 9 October 1917 to 28 April 1936. During his reign, the 1919 revolution began, and the British had to end Egypt's status as a protectorate and declare it an independent country with sovereignty. Independence was declared on 15 March 1922. Also during his reign, the first public ministry was established in January 1924, headed by Sa`d Zaghlul. King Fu`ad had a number of important accomplishments, and for this reason this photo was chosen – to manifest King Fu`ad's concern with roads, especially the royal road towards the Fayum Directorate.
keywords: King Fu`ad; Fayum Directorate; new roads; The Royal Road

d6720426-2881-5b4a-8e11-89649a430aa6.name: *Loie Fuller: the serpentine dance*
d6720426-2881-5b4a-8e11-89649a430aa6.short_description: Mary Louise Fuller was an American dancer who lived in Europe for many years. As an artist, she was inspired by her travels and by new inventions - the dance of the veils (the "serpentine" dance) mixes Arab influences with light tricks using electricity. Loie Fuller was an important influence in the Art Nouveau and Symbolist movements, and helped train other great artists such as Isadora Duncan. The "serpentine dance" was imitated by many artists, and inspired the first cinematographers, such as the Lumière brothers, who dedicated a short film to it.
keywords: Dance; Orientalism; electricity

d6cffdd2-cbd5-5bf7-bd67-0a2b5084a2cc.name: In Tunis, the families of the Italian men drafted for the war waiting to get their daily allowance from the Italian government
d6cffdd2-cbd5-5bf7-bd67-0a2b5084a2cc.short_description: According to a booklet published in 1917 by the Tunisian branch of the Dante Alighieri Society and quoted by historian Adriano Salmieri (see his contribution to the volume *Mestieri e professioni degli italiani di Tunisia* – *Métiers et professions des Italiens de Tunisie, a cura di S. Finzi, Tunisi: Finzi*, 2003), by the end of April 1917 11,146 Italians in Tunisia had been drafted for the war, and 700 had died. According to the same source, in 1917 in Tunisia the Italian government was paying daily allowances to almost 5,000 destitute families of drafted soldiers.

d6e29c37-877d-59fc-ba89-0136adddb6e7.description: At the end of the 19th and during the first decade of the 20th century Pirot kilims served as unavoidable decor in public buildings and in important public manifestations. An official wedding photo of King Alexander Obrenović of Serbia and Queen Draga, shows a royal couple standing on the Pirot kilims, used as floor coverings in this solemn occasion as distinguished national products. The official photograph, taken on 4 August 1900 by the court photographer Milan Jovanović, was issued on a poster by the bookstore of Sreten J. Djordjević and printed by the State Printing House of the Kingdom of Serbia.

d7bf5b87-41a9-54ad-80be-78334ba1edff.short_description: Between 1841 and 1844, Adolphe Thiers had a 33km long city wall built to protect Paris. These "fortif'" (fortifications), which were proved to be useless during the war in 1870, soon became inhabited by the poor. It was an area made up of shacks, and soon became a lawless zone. The demolition of the "fortif" began in Clignancourt in 1919, in order to make way for new urbanisation projects and disperse the inhabitants. In this photograph, we can see the neighbourhood children contributing to the works.
keywords: Cities; demolition; fortifications; urbanisation

d7e2a6e6-e1c7-57b6-a8e7-ae3661622194.name: Photograph of the Mahmal ceremony
d7e2a6e6-e1c7-57b6-a8e7-ae3661622194.short_description: This photograph shows the Mahmal preparing to leave Cairo for Mecca. It is has the title: '*Le Mahmal no 140*' with the signature of Abdullah Freres. Abdullah Frères were three Ottoman Armenian brothers who ran photographic studios in Istanbul, Cairo and Izmir. In 1862 they were named official royal photographers to the Ottoman court with the entitlement to use the royal monogram. Their studio operated between 1858-99 and while they were appointed to photograph Sultan Abdülaziz and Sultan Abdülhamid II, they were also commissioned to document aspects of the Ottoman Empire. This image was also reproduced on postcards and was also used in Saleh Soubhy’s *Pèlerinage à la Mecque et à Médine*. Visible on the mahmal is the date 1304 (AH), with part of the name of the Khedive Muhammd Tawfiq, meaning that the Mahmal was sent by order of Sultan Abdülhamid II.
d7e2a6e6-e1c7-57b6-a8e7-ae3661622194.holder: Khalili Family Trust – Hajj and the Arts of Pilgrimage Collection
d7e2a6e6-e1c7-57b6-a8e7-ae3661622194.method_for_datation: The photograph is signed. The date must be AH 1304 (AD 1886), the date visible on the mahmal, or soon after.
d7e2a6e6-e1c7-57b6-a8e7-ae3661622194.author: Qaisra Khan

d86bffa6-0320-50d5-b0a4-c47134d7d642.name: Water pumping equipment in Kağıthane, Istanbul
d86bffa6-0320-50d5-b0a4-c47134d7d642.short_description: During the 19th century, new technologies radically transformed both travel and communications. Cendere Hamidian Water Pump Station was built by Abdülhamid II in 1902 at an altitude of 34 metres above sea level. With its function, architectural design and mechanical equipment, the station is a unique monument to the history of the architecture industry in the Ottoman Empire. It pumped to Balmumcu and Beşiktaş – in the direction of Tophane, moving water coming from 20 different pipes in Kağıthane using steam pump machines.

d8d34fe2-1034-53c0-ae9e-ca9794a01c63.name: Railway Bridge from Anatolia
d8d34fe2-1034-53c0-ae9e-ca9794a01c63.short_description: During the 19th century, new technologies radically transformed both travel and communications. The first railway in Anatolia was constructed between Izmir and Aydin. Ottoman railways were mainly built during the period of Abdülhamid II. The first railway in the Republic of Turkey was part of the İzmir-Aydın line, founded by a British company in 1860. The İzmir-Kasaba line was built in 1865, the Rumeli line in 1869-77, the Anatolia-Baghdad line in 1872 and the Mudanya-Bursa line in 1892.

d9e955c1-2a6e-5af6-be73-7eb332bb3d48.name: Ausbootung in Haifa. (Disembarking in Haifa)
d9e955c1-2a6e-5af6-be73-7eb332bb3d48.description: The photograph shows Haifa’s waterfront railway facilities. A passenger train stands directly beside the stone quay, while a large crowd gathers between the railway carriages and the water and on a boat. One-third of the area was filled with pavilions designed by famous Italian architects. The exhibition cost was over twelve million lire. This photograph shows two Turkish women, probably mother and daughter, in formal dress.

dd29cce2-b0da-5709-8418-0fcea165baa5.description: San Remo Conference, April 1920. In this hall, the voices of colonial powers of the early 20th century were heard, strangers to the land, yet deciding its fate.

ddc859b5-2660-59d5-a43e-bea3692d92db.name: Italian stonecutters in Tunisia
ddc859b5-2660-59d5-a43e-bea3692d92db.short_description: At the turn of the twentieth century, the Italian community in Tunisia included large numbers of masons, stonecutters, diggers and other manual workers. In this period, most of Italian migrants preferred to seek their fortunes in the Americas and in other European countries. Those who migrated to North Africa were only a small percentage, nonetheless they amounted to dozens of thousands.

dddd9f2e-9bbf-52e9-b0c9-6daa195c732b.name: View of Jebel Kuruntul taken from the Jericho Plain
dddd9f2e-9bbf-52e9-b0c9-6daa195c732b.description: A view of Jebel Kuruntul from the Jericho plain with the remains of Mamluk sugar mills and aqueducts in the middle distance. Charles Warren describes the scene in his book *Underground Jerusalem*, AH 1293 / AD 1876: p 167, and pp 185–189. This picture was taken from Warren's campsite. “Our way lay over some low swelling hills, on which the ruins of the sugar mills remain, and the aqueduct which brought water to work them from ‘Ain ed Duk. These mills appear to have been put up after the Moslem conquest, when the plain of Jericho was in a high state of cultivation; even as late as the 12th century it was accounted the garden of Palestine”: 186.

dde582f0-5bed-53bd-adaa-91e404fab4de.name: Orfella. The kaimacan Mohàmmed-el-Jesir [Qaimaqan Muhammad al-Jazir] and Notables Observe Studies on Subterranean Water of Wadi Beni Ulid Requested from the Italian Mission
dde582f0-5bed-53bd-adaa-91e404fab4de.short_description: In 1911, right before the beginning of Italy’s colonial war in Libya, an expert in sulphur mining, Ignazio Sanfilippo, headed a mission to Libya to look for mineral resources (in particular, for sulphur mines). The mission was sponsored by the Libyan branch of the Banca di Roma (one of the most important Italian banks, which supported Italian colonial expansion in Libya), and it was encouraged by the Italian government. In 1910, Sanfilippo had already headed another Italian mission to Libya. He had been secretly charged by the Minister of Foreign Affairs to look for sulphur mines and the Banca di Roma had helped organising the mission.
dde582f0-5bed-53bd-adaa-91e404fab4de.author: Giulia Barrera

de4d9eaf-e78d-5c74-9efd-dd68d0c7fae9.name: Entrance of the Hammam of the Mouassine Mosque (Marrakech)
de4d9eaf-e78d-5c74-9efd-dd68d0c7fae9.description: The entrance to the *hammam* of the Mouassine Mosque in Marrakech is situated within an area of the city that dates back to antiquity. This area demonstrates the interconnection between water, buildings and the quality of life of the inhabitants of the medina. The Mouassine complex was constructed during the Saadian period in the 16th century. The architectural design of the building was conceived with the intention of creating a multifunctional civic foundation, thereby ensuring its versatility in terms of utilisation. The complex included a mosque, fountain, hammam, madrasa and public amenities. The entrance to the hammam is modest and integrated into the urban fabric, reflecting the traditional Moroccan approach to architecture where public buildings are an integral part of the city.
de4d9eaf-e78d-5c74-9efd-dd68d0c7fae9.author: Yelyzaveta Basysta
keywords: Water; Mosque; Photography; Marrakech.

df551296-3682-582b-a97b-05ba149fa548.name: Constant Delessert, double exposure
df551296-3682-582b-a97b-05ba149fa548.description: Adrien Constant de Rebecque, better known as Constant Delessert, was a typical child of the nineteenth century, an age of great change. In his role as a pioneer of photography he experimented with various techniques, such as double exposure. This allowed Delessert to arrange portraits and self-portraits in such as a manner that it looked like two individuals were interacting, although, in fact, it was the same person exposed twice in short sequence but in different roles. In the present picture Delessert is looking at himself while reading. The play with cultural stereotypes – his double exposures include pictures of servants, portrait painters as well as beggars – in combination with the, often delayed, realization that one is dealing with one and the same person, makes this series so remarkable. Together with other museums, the Swiss National Museum was able to purchase ten albums with works by Constant Delessert at an auction, five of which are now in the National Museum collection. They contain portraits, natural scenes, architectural images as well as street views. They visualize the Switzerland of Delessert’s era in a remarkable way. Delessert, who came from an affluent family, also staged and documented with the help of images of poor people, servants and peasants how, in those days, clothing embodied visible social boundaries.
keywords: photography; Constant Delessert; double exposure; self-portrait
materials: Photography; double exposure; albumen print on paper; mounted (pasted)

dfe6e123-1970-5707-8279-08002d40fd1f.name: Ottoman Clothing Album
dfe6e123-1970-5707-8279-08002d40fd1f.short_description: With the political developments of the 19th century, interest in the East increased steadily in the western world. Everything belonging to the East was the centre of interest for western observers. As a result, close to 160 artists visited Istanbul in the 19th century. Pascal Sébah (1823-86) was a pioneer photographer who worked in Istanbul. Sébah opened a photography studio known as "El Chark " in Pera in 1857. The studio's most successful period started with the Vienna Universal Exhibition in 1873. Sébah formed a partnership with Joaillier Polycarpe in 1885. In 1899, the two partners bought Abdullah Frères's archives. For the Vienna Universal Exhibition in 1873, Pascal Sébah prepared *The Ottoman Clothing Album* to be exhibited at the Ottoman Stand.

e055e6ed-ffba-5b33-a42a-7f9060dc3802.name: Paul Draneht, his wife Adele Casati and their daughter Despina
e055e6ed-ffba-5b33-a42a-7f9060dc3802.short_description:
Paul Draneht (1815-1894) was born in Nicosia (Cyprus) as Pavlos Pavlidis. He was the child of a Greek Christian Orthodox family who fled Cyprus to escape the clashes between Greeks and Turks and then took refuge in Egypt.  
The Khedive of Egypt sent him to study in France. He later had a brilliant career in service to the Khedive participating in the negotiations on the opening of the Suez Canal. He became superintendent of the Egyptian Opera Theatre and commissioned the opera Aida to the Italian composer Giuseppe Verdi.  
Paul Draneht married Adelaide Casati, the daughter of a cello player who performed at the Aida premiere. Their daughter Despina Draneht married a Greek businessman, Emmanuel Zervudachi.
e055e6ed-ffba-5b33-a42a-7f9060dc3802.author: Massimiliano Cremona, Ignazio Galella

e0cacb7c-8356-5070-a4ca-e40684822c68.name: Solomon’s Pools
e0cacb7c-8356-5070-a4ca-e40684822c68.description: The so-called Solomon's Pools at Artas near Bethlehem. These pools date from the Roman period and have a complex history of use, disuse and reuse lasting into the Mandate period. They were significantly refurbished in the Mamluk and early Ottoman periods. They were built to bring water into Jerusalem through a series of pipes and aqueducts, a process facilitated by the slightly higher ground at Artas relative to Jerusalem, and also for use in Artas and Bethlehem. They are fed by four nearby springs.

e0f05556-5282-5134-9488-cb1139890651.name: 'Jerusalem Railway Station. 325. La Gare'
e0f05556-5282-5134-9488-cb1139890651.description: This is a cropped albumen print made from an original negative by the American Colony. It may be the same as the picture No. 28 on page 2 in "1911 Revised and Enlarged Catalogue of Lantern Slides made by the American Colony, Jerusalem..." (published by Vester & Co., Jerusalem). The picture shows the Baldwin locomotive No. 3  on the right with "Ramleh" on a plaque on its side. On the left are three carriages, one with the letters "J.J" (i.e. the Jaffa-Jerusalem line) on its side. The Jerusalem train station building can be seen behind the carriages, with a pole on its roof for a flag. Three engineers and one local man can be seen in the picture."American Colony, Jerusalem" appears in the lower right-hand corner. The letter "s" in Jerusalem is inverted. Similar inverted letters appeared in another American Colony print (see P 1734). In a band at the bottom of the print: "Jerusalem Railway Station 325 La Gare". A partly scratched out plate number "18" or 1S" appears in the lower left-hand corner.

e1be7517-b6b1-576b-8acd-653f24c29ba9.name: *Hijaz Railway Station, Damascus*
e1be7517-b6b1-576b-8acd-653f24c29ba9.short_description: The Hijaz station was originally built in 1903 to provide faster transportation for Pilgrims to Medina. So the today closed-down railway station used to be an essential transport and communication link. Furthermore it was built to integrate aloof provinces better into the Ottoman state and hence establish a closer political and economic connection. The new building completed in 1917 also embodies a desire for innovation in terms of design: its architecture is a mix between traditional local Ottoman elements and monumentalizing features of historicism.
e1be7517-b6b1-576b-8acd-653f24c29ba9.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum, State Museums

e1f071ed-6026-5f1b-bac8-49caf60ecd7a.name: Migration preparations from Lemnos island to Turkey
e1f071ed-6026-5f1b-bac8-49caf60ecd7a.short_description: The 1923 population exchange between Greece and Turkey was based upon religious identity, and involved the Greek Orthodox citizens of Turkey and the Muslim citizens of Greece. The "Convention Concerning the Exchange of Greek and Turkish Populations" was signed at Lausanne, Switzerland, on 30 January 1923, by the governments of Greece and Turkey. During the migration waves during the 1896-97 riots in Crete, 40,000 Cretan Muslims had to migrate to territories under Ottoman rule: Lebanon, Syria and Anatolia. This photograph pertains to migration preparations from Lemnos to Turkey in 1924.
e1f071ed-6026-5f1b-bac8-49caf60ecd7a.holder: Population Exchange Museum (The Foundation of Lausanne Treaty Emigrants)

e3029e51-8121-5e09-b08a-bd958da4cd09.name: 'The first railway engine in Tripoli'
e3029e51-8121-5e09-b08a-bd958da4cd09.short_description:
The railway in a colonial context was much more than a means of transport: it was a powerful symbol of modernity, of technological superiority of the colonisers over the colonised, and of mastery over the territory. The construction of railways in colonial situations was often celebrated by the colonialists’ popular press or in postcards, as in this case.  
In Libya, the Italians started building railroads from the first months of colonial rule. The first lines, inaugurated in 1912, connected Tripoli with Ain Zara (11 kms) and to Zanzur (39 kms). By the end of 1915, the railway lines in Libya amounted to 180 kilometres.
e3029e51-8121-5e09-b08a-bd958da4cd09.author: Giulia Barrera

e5e027ae-6390-53b1-82f7-668b99a7615c.name: Slave market
e5e027ae-6390-53b1-82f7-668b99a7615c.short_description: This souk, Souk el-Birka, was built by Youssef Dey in the early 17th century in the Tunis medina, and was used for the purpose of selling slaves. It was served, until the 16th century, by seasonal carriages from sub-Saharan Africa. By 1850, the number of slaves and their descendants in Tunisia was estimated to be around 80,000. The majority did agricultural work in the oases in the south, but many were also working in domestic roles in bourgeois households and the bey's residence. In 1841 Ahmed Bey banned the sale of slaves and demolished the stores reserved for this purpose, and in 1842 he abolished slavery.

e68c9926-6b22-5aab-b71e-e3faba6e95e4.name: Halabja, Iraq
e68c9926-6b22-5aab-b71e-e3faba6e95e4.description: As demonstrated in this image, the city landscape of Halabja, in Iraq, features Kurdish individuals attired in traditional attire, namely knickers and turbans, traversing the city's souk. In the immediate foreground of the scene is depicted a pitcher of water, offered for the passers-by's use. On March 16, 1988, Halabja was the victim of a large-scale chemical attack by Saddam Hussein's army, which killed thousands and injured many more. The attacks destroyed the city, and parts of the city remained contaminated by the toxic gases for decades to come. Little remains of the city life seen in the image.

Making pasta was hard work. In Tunisia, the industrialization of pasta production started only in the 20th century.

e6ce0745-bf5d-5a64-ab65-c5f97224e8ef.short_description: On the occasion of the International Exhibition of Rome in 1911, the complex of the "Baths of Diocletian” was restored under the direction of the archeologist and topographer Rodolfo Lanciani. The site housed the Archaeological Exhibition dedicated to the Roman culture in the Imperial Era with a particular interest for its positive influence on the ex provinces. Every single nation participated through original reproductions of archaeological materials, often lost. The photo shows material evidence and casts coming from Greece.

e7371a10-6fed-5f3b-b834-5b48379f0edf.name: Celebrations outside the station.
e7371a10-6fed-5f3b-b834-5b48379f0edf.description: The German field-postcard part of the German series Die Türkei im Weltkriege (Turkey in the World War) records the procession organised outside Damascus’s Hijaz Railway Station following the arrival of Jamal Pasha during the First World War. According to the printed caption, a military band leads cadets, military school pupils and members of the Jugendwehr, or youth corps, around the station. Their participation reflects the wartime mobilisation of education and youth to physical training and elementary military preparation. The station functions here as a ceremonial entrance to Damascus, where military authority and public spectacle took place. Beside the station stands the Izzat al Malla Building, one of the prominent structures in the developing Halbouni district adjacent to the station.

e80567bb-4a41-5dd5-a8c2-8530ecf7b427.name: Abdelaziz Thâalbi (Abdelaziz al-Thalibi)
e80567bb-4a41-5dd5-a8c2-8530ecf7b427.short_description: Born in Tunis in 1876, Abdelaziz Thâalbi (Abdelaziz al-Thalibi) was a Tunisian politician. In 1920, he became the founder of the political party Destour, and participated in all the first fights of the nationalist movement. This activism caused him to be sent into exile in 1912, not for the first time, with six other nationalist politicians. In 1920 he wrote and published the manifesto La Tunisie Martyre with Ahmed Sakka, for which he was arrested on 31 July and taken to Tunis. However, feeling threatened there, he fled and left Tunisia once again in 1923. Destourian militants in Tunisia kept calling for his return, which finally happened in July 1937, 14 years after being forced into exile. However, upon his return he entered into conflict with Neo-Destour politicians, led by Bourguiba. He died on 1 October 1944, and his funeral was an opportunity for the Neo-Destour movement, as well as all the fringes of the nationalist movement to gather, and pay tribute to one of the founding fathers of Tunisian nationalism
e80567bb-4a41-5dd5-a8c2-8530ecf7b427.holder: Institut Supérieur d’Histoire Contemporaine de la Tunisie
e80567bb-4a41-5dd5-a8c2-8530ecf7b427.author: Bechir Yazidi
keywords: The Young Tunisians movement; "La Tunisie Martyre"

e8867b07-6d42-5182-8664-51768b182008.name: Abd al-Kader at Amboise
e8867b07-6d42-5182-8664-51768b182008.short_description: Emir 'Abd al-Kader was the symbol of Algerian resistance to the French occupation from 1832 to 1847. After his resignation in 1847, he was taken to the Château de Pau, followed by hundreds of people, where he was detained until he was moved to the Château d'Amboise. His behaviour during his time in captivity attracted the admiration of the French, who saw him as a romantic hero: he studied, meditated, and was always ready to receive visitors. The various portraits and photographs of him that were produced portrayed him as a pious man rather than the warrior he had been. In 1852, the Prince Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte went to Amboise to officially announce the end of his captivity.
keywords: Diplomacy; Algeria; France; colonies; 'Abd al-Kader

e8c3f98d-322b-5f12-ac61-73a1b189f9cc.name: Station du Chemin de fer El-Mina. Tripoli, Syrie (El-Mina Railway Station, Tripoli, Syria)
e8c3f98d-322b-5f12-ac61-73a1b189f9cc.description: El-Mina railway station at Tripoli opened in 1911, initially connecting Tripoli with Homs by a single-track gauge. The D.H.P.’s Tripoli–Homs line was approximately 102 km long. Its position at El-Mina (the port of Tripoli) provided the Syrian interior with a direct railway connection to the Mediterranean. The commercial consequences were already apparent in 1912 when British Foreign Office trade reports recorded that goods including wool, hides, liquorice root and cotton, which had previously been exported through Beirut, were increasingly passed through Tripoli after the railway opened.

ec43977b-e543-5455-bbeb-c0f1565cf50d.name: Photograph of the Krushevo Revolutionary Squad
ec43977b-e543-5455-bbeb-c0f1565cf50d.short_description: The Krushevo Revolutionary Squad played an active role in the Uprising of Ilinden, which broke out on 2 August 1903. The main battles of the uprising were waged in the Bitola Revolutionary Region, more precisely, in the town of Krushevo. Pitu Guli (1865–1903) was leader of the squad. He was a Vlach from Krushevo who was fully devoted to the idea of an autonomous Macedonia from an early age. It is noteworthy that not all revolutionaries taking part in the uprising were Macedonians. Vlachs from the Krushevo region were also actively involved in the battles. The Krushevo Squad played a crucial role in taking over of the town. Together with troops from other parts of Macedonia, they managed to liberate the town and declare the Krushevo Republic. Pitu Guli lost his life defending the Krushevo Republic on 12 August 1903.
ec43977b-e543-5455-bbeb-c0f1565cf50d.author: Nada Andonovska (author), Dragan Georgiev, historian (consultant)

ecbd97bc-85ed-53b3-ab05-ca13100e4055.name: Reconstruction of Ancyra Temple at the Rome International Exhibition, 1911
ecbd97bc-85ed-53b3-ab05-ca13100e4055.short_description: Over the centuries the Baths of Diocletian, sacked by the barbarians of Alaric, were abandoned and restored several times. In 1563, Pope Paul IV commissioned Michelangelo to transform it into a church “Santa Maria degli Angeli”. In 1749 the architect Vanvitelli rebuilt it again. For the International Exhibition of Rome in 1911, the complex of the "Baths of Diocletian” was restored again under the direction of Rodolfo Lanciani for the International Exhibition of Rome in 1911, to host the Archaeological Exhibition dedicated to Roman culture in the Imperial Era with a particular interest for its positive influence on the "ex provinces". The most incredible reconstruction on display was the Temple of Ancyra (ancient capital of Galatia, in the centre of Minor Asia) dedicated to Augustus and the goddess Roma, based on casts taken by the archaeologist Azeglio Berretti. Included in the display are the famous engraved inscription on bronze tablets, the so-called "Res Gestae” that represents the testament of emperor Augustus.

ed280684-f7be-5238-afc4-1fd992c55380.name: An old exhibition from Tiled Kiosk
ed280684-f7be-5238-afc4-1fd992c55380.short_description: The Tiled Kiosk is a pavilion set within the outer walls of Topkapı Palace and dates from 1472. It was built by the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II as a pleasure palace or kiosk. The building was used as the Imperial Museum between 1875 and 1891. In 1953, it was opened to the public as a museum of Turkish and Islamic art, and was later incorporated into the Istanbul Archaeology Museums. The collections of the Tiled Kiosk Museum consist of about 2000 artefacts belonging to the Seljuk and Ottoman eras, dating from the 11th-20th centuries. These artefacts include those that existed when the museum was incorporated into the İstanbul Archaeological Museums due to its closeness and those acquired through excavations, purchases, donations and confiscations.

ef67fa8c-4ff1-55bf-83f3-ae6118113aaa.description:
This picture was taken in Tetouan during a trip of the painter Joaquín Sorolla and his friends to Morocco in 1919. Sorolla's family and friends were portrayed with local people, a highlight of which is the Moor Selam and other characters and exotic animals, such as the monkey. Especially interesting is her daughter Helena who appeared in a Moorish costume.  
This travel appeared in the newspapers El Confidencial and ABC which also published this photograph.  
This family trip brought back memories and objects. The painter's daughter, Helena, had their little Moorish corner on the stairs of the house which is now the Sorolla Museum. A table, a chest, tambourines, fabrics, jewellery were bought back as souvenirs.

The museum was founded by decree in 1891 as the Imperial Museum. The first curator and founder of the museum was Osman Hamdi. Hamdi began construction of the main building in 1881, and it achieved its present neo-Greek form in 1908. The architect was Alexander Vallaury. It is one of the prominent structures built in the neoclassical style in Istanbul. Osman Hamdi, during his tenure as museum director, launched the first Turkish scientific excavations. He carried out archaeological excavations at Mount Nemrut, Laguna and Sidon.

f243ea50-61a0-52e5-843b-6c277186a513.name: Caiffa (Palestine), Date de l´installation du Chemin de fer du Hedjaz. Memorial Monument (The Exalted Column Memorial Monument, the beginning of the construction of the Hijaz Railway, Haifa, Palestine)
f243ea50-61a0-52e5-843b-6c277186a513.description: The Exalted Column, Haifa, known in Ottoman Turkish as Sütūn-u ʿĀlī and in Arabic as al-’Amud al-’Ali (العمود العالي), is a monument erected in 1903 to commemorate the beginning of construction of the Haifa–Dar’a railway branch, part of the Hijaz Railway project. The monument is generally attributed to Raimondo D’Aronco, the Italian architect who served the Ottoman court during the reign of Sultan Abdülhamid II. Haifa’s location offered significant advantages over the nearby port of Acre. Connecting the railway to Haifa enabled construction materials, coal, machinery and other supplies to be delivered by sea and transported inland. It also created a transport corridor through which agricultural produce and commercial goods from inland Syria and Palestine could reach the Mediterranean coast.

f5030f3c-8af5-552d-8913-157bc3d6732c.name: Marina Square, Reem Island
f5030f3c-8af5-552d-8913-157bc3d6732c.description: This image of Marina Square on Reem Island (Abu Dhabi) reflects the transformation of modern Arab cities, where architecture and urban planning increasingly embrace blue spaces: areas designed around proximity to water. Alongside residential towers, these coastal developments integrate museums, cultural centres, promenades, and commercial hubs, merging urban living with leisure and cultural life. In many contemporary Arab cities, waterfront development symbolises progress, prosperity, and global connectivity, echoing the historic relationship between water and civilisation in the region. Just as ancient settlements flourished near rivers and coasts, today’s skylines continue to grow along the shores, redefining how water shapes identity, lifestyles, and the rhythms of urban experience.

f562fef5-27de-5b9d-af36-fde217967898.name: Station de chemin de fer du port de Beyrouth (Beirut Railway Station)
f562fef5-27de-5b9d-af36-fde217967898.description: Beirut Port Train Station was established in 1903 when the railway infrastructure of Beirut was extended to reach the harbour docks during the expansion of the D.H.P. network. The port station was created to facilitate the transfer of goods arriving by sea into the railway system. This connection formed part of a wider phase of railway expansion following the renewal of the company’s concession in 1887. Construction in Rayak began in 1902 and then reached Hama. In 1903, Beirut Station was connected directly with the Beirut quay through this station. The project subsequently extended the network from the Mediterranean to the interior by the Hama–Aleppo and Homs–Tripoli branches between 1905 and 1911.
